articles.title: Pentagon policy chief says NATO allies back Europe defence shift
articles.body:
NATO allies backing Europe defence shift, says Pentagon policy chief
- The Pentagon's top policy official says NATO allies support Europe's shift to non-nuclear defence and are increasing their defence investments under the 'NATO 3.0' vision.
- The US is reviewing troop levels in Europe, currently about 80,000, while ensuring allies step up before any troop reductions to avoid security risks.
- Allies have responded positively to US outreach, buying US-made weapons and strengthening domestic defence, despite tensions over US military use of bases and political disagreements.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – As European capitals brace themselves for US troop cuts, the Pentagon’s top policy official is telling lawmakers in Washington that allies are on board with a vision of “NATO 3.0”, in which Europe maintains its own non-nuclear defence.
An ongoing six-month review of American troop levels in Europe is at the stage where the US Defence Department is “showing them how to step up and then helping them to do so”, Undersecretary of Defence for Policy Elbridge Colby told the Senate Armed Services Committee in a statement released on Sept 28 but dated Sept 22.
The department submitted a 16-page document to committee members after Colby delivered a required briefing on the administration’s 2026 National Defence Strategy, drawing bipartisan criticism for what members of Congress saw as a lack of transparency.
In 2025, lawmakers used the Pentagon’s annual policy Bill to restrict the administration’s ability to cut the US presence in Europe below 76,000 troops without engaging in extensive consultations with allies and Congress and taking steps to mitigate any security risks to the alliance. The US has about 80,000 troops in Europe.
Europeans have expressed concerns that the US could withdraw troops and equipment from the continent, in a reorganisation that the Trump administration calls NATO 3.0, before allies are ready to replace them – creating new vulnerabilities at a time when Russia poses a continued threat.
President Donald Trump has complained that NATO allies were unwilling to join the war in Iran, which he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu started without consultations.
In response, allies placed limits on the US military’s use of their bases and airspace.
The US President has signalled his intention to punish allies for this perceived disloyalty.
According to Colby’s missive, the administration’s campaign for increased burden-sharing among allies “appears to be working”, with allies increasing their investments in defence, buying US-made weapons and bolstering their domestic defence industries.
Colby advised lawmakers that “allies have typically responded constructively to the department’s outreach”, through conversations with US officials and in “substantive responses” to a questionnaire submitted to allied capitals that sought to assess not only their strategic contributions, but also their loyalty to the President’s policies. BLOOMBERG

articles.title: Russian nuclear-capable bomber plane crashes, killing six people
articles.body:
Russian Tu-95 nuclear-capable bomber plane crashes, killing six people
Tu-95 plane crashed during a training flight in an uninhabited area of Amur region, Defence Ministry says.
A Russian military aircraft has crashed in the eastern region of Amur, killing at least six crew members and leaving one hospitalised, according to Russia’s Ministry of Defence.
Russian state media on Tuesday cited the ministry as saying the Tu-95 plane crashed during a training flight in an uninhabited area of Amur, a region bordering China.
The plane was flying without ammunition, according to the TASS state-run news agency.
Interfax news agency quoted Russia’s military as saying that an Aerospace Forces commission had been dispatched “to the crash site to establish all the circumstances of the incident”.
Unverified social media videos of the purported crash aftermath showed large amounts of smoke rising from the burning aircraft.
The Tupolev Tu-95 is a large, Soviet-era bomber aircraft that can carry, launch and deliver nuclear weapons.
It was first flown in 1952 but was only introduced into service in 1956 and remains in use, often by the Russian military in routine military exercises.
This is not the first time aircraft have gone down in Russia’s Far East. In July last year, an Antonov An-24 plane crashed in poor weather conditions on its way to the town of Tynda, killing all 48 people on board.
In August 2021, a Mil Mi-8 crashed in the Kamchatka Peninsula of Russia with 16 people on board, most of whom were tourists.

articles.title: Kataib Hezbollah threatens Iraq govt over Iran airline ban
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Kataib Hezbollah threatens to bring down Iraqi govt over Iranian airline ban
A powerful Iran-backed militia in Iraq on Monday threatened to bring down the government if it continued to bar Iranian flights from entering the country in line with recent US sanctions.
The Kataib Hezbollah warning came after several countries began restricting Iranian airlines from operating at their airports as sweeping new US sanctions targeting Iran's aviation sector came into force on 23 September.
"We warn Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi and those behind him that any government that does not work in the interests of the people will be brought down by all means," Kataib Hezbollah’s security official Abu Mujhaid al-Assaf wrote in a social media post.
"If the air blockade on Iran continues after the first of next month, our people will take a clear position, which could include closing the border crossings of countries participating in the blockade of the Iranian people," continued al-Assaf. He did not explicitly name the countries he was referring to, leaving it unclear which border crossings he was threatening to close.
All four Iraqi airports that had been operating flights to and from Iran suspended them, significantly expanding restrictions first imposed in Baghdad.
But flights from Iran to and from Najaf have resumed under a US waiver.
Iraq's ambassador to Iran Yasser al-Hajjaj reportedly said on Monday that Iraq had not banned flights but foreign companies were refusing to provide services to Iranian carriers for fear of US sanctions.
The Iraqi state news agency INA said that only Iraqi Airways would now operate flights to and from Najaf.
Iraq is an important market for Iranian airlines, which carry Iranian pilgrims to Shia shrines in Najaf and Karbala, and Iraqi travellers in the opposite direction.
"The Iraqi people will celebrate on the 30th of this month by expelling the occupying US and NATO forces from Iraq," al-Assaf said, referring to the United States completing its military pullout from Iraq after a decades-long presence following the 2003 invasion.
He said the "Islamic Resistance in Iraq" would monitor Iraqi airspace to ensure it was not violated by hostile aircraft, warning: "We will issue a warning first and then shoot them down." He added that the prime minister’s office, under its current leadership, should not become a "cashier" for US violations after 1 October.
Kataib Hezbollah was not officially given seats in al-Zaidi’s cabinet, as al-Zaidi agreed to exclude militia-aligned actors from his government to secure international support and avoid immediate US sanctions, ending months of political stalemate in Iraq.
While Kataib Hezbollah is officially part of Iraq’s state-funded security apparatus through the Popular Mobilisation Forces, it enjoys a large level of autonomy.
Iraq has long played a delicate balancing act in its relations with Washington and Tehran, which both still yield significant political and military influence in the country.
The US backs al-Zaidi’s government and is pressuring it to disarm Iran-backed factions and bring all arms under state control. While most groups have agreed to surrender their weapons and integrate with the state, Kataib Hezbollah has refused to disarm.
When the US-Israel war on Iran broke out, deadly US-Israeli airstrikes hit bases belonging to Iran-backed militias in Iraq which in turn targeted US interests, including Washington’s embassy and bases hosting US forces.

articles.title: Zircon and ballistic missiles launched by Russia neutralized over Ukraine - details from Air Force
articles.body:
Zircon and ballistic missiles launched by Russia neutralized over Ukraine - details from Air Force
Kyiv • UNN
During the night of September 29, Russia launched a Zircon-type missile, two ballistic missiles, and 152 drones at Ukraine. Air defense destroyed 109 targets, including the missiles.
Russia struck Ukraine during the night of September 29 with a Zircon-type missile, two ballistic missiles, and 152 drones; all the missiles—the Zircon and the two ballistic missiles—as well as 106 drones were shot down or suppressed. UNN reports this, citing data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
What Russia attacked with and from where
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of September 29 (from 18:00 on September 28), the enemy attacked with a Zircon/Oniks anti-ship missile from Russia’s Kursk Region; two Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles from Russia’s Kursk Region; and 152 Shahed-type attack UAVs (82 of them jet-powered), Gerbera UAVs, and Parodiya-type decoy drones from the following directions: Oryol, Millerovo, Kursk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk—in Russia; the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk; Hvardiiske; and Chauda—the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea.
How many were destroyed
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense forces shot down/suppressed 109 targets:
-  1 Zircon/Oniks anti-ship missile; 
-  2 Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles; 
-  106 enemy Shahed-type and Gerbera UAVs and drones of other types. 
Hits by the enemy’s air attack weapons were recorded at 24 locations, as well as the سقوط of downed targets (debris) at 16 locations.
The attack is ongoing; several enemy UAVs are in the airspace.

articles.title: Lavrov destroys BBC’s ‘hybrid war’ play (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Lavrov destroys BBC’s ‘hybrid war’ play (VIDEO)
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has treated an accusation from a BBC correspondent with the contempt expected of a veteran diplomat.
The British state broadcaster’s Steve Rosenberg asked Lavrov if he would admit “that Russia is waging a covert hybrid war against European countries?”
“Are you referring to when we destroy the drones and missiles that Britain and continental Europe supply to Ukraine, which are then fired at us?” the Russian foreign minister retorted. “Is that what you mean by hybrid war?”
Rosenberg then dropped his line of questioning and switched to criticizing Russia for its use of “brute force” in Ukraine.
BBC’s Rosenberg: Do you admit that Russia is waging a covert hybrid war against European countries?
Lavrov: Are you referring to when we destroy the drones and missiles that Britain and continental Europe supply to Ukraine, which are then fired at us? Is that what you mean by… pic.twitter.com/XkLe49xcNX
“If you are referring to the destruction of infrastructure used by the [Ukrainian] Nazi regime – with Western support – to wage war against the Russian Federation, then we are resorting to hard power to neutralize this direct threat to us,” Lavrov replied.
Rosenberg’s question to Russia’s top diplomat followed several days of high-pitch war hysteria in the UK press, including a significantly over-reported ‘security incident’ near an RAF base.
European politicians regularly describe drone sightings, fires and accidents at weapons factories, and even natural disasters as examples of a Russian “hybrid war” against the West. The term “hybrid war” is typically used in reporting cases where no hard evidence exists, as was the case when a small quadcopter drone was discovered next to a Ukrainian transport plane at Leipzig Airport in Germany last month.
In the latest such incident, Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna blamed Russia on Tuesday for a fire at a drone factory in Tallinn last month. Although the Kremlin has denied any role in the blaze, the UK, France, Latvia, Lithuania, and Sweden all backed Tsahkna’s story and pledged on Tuesday to increase military aid to Kiev.
Amid an upsurge in supposed “hybrid war” incidents, Western military leaders have escalated their war rhetoric, with members of the UK’s Labour and Conservative parties both claiming last week that a military clash with Russia is inevitable, and Spanish media claiming that Italy, France, and Spain are all at risk of a Russian drone attack from the Mediterranean Sea. The latter claim, though widely echoed across the international press, was summarily debunked by senior French and Italian officials.
“We have no intention to fight with Europe…that is utter nonsense,” Lavrov told journalists at the UN General Assembly on Saturday. “But Europe is preparing for war with us, and each day they reaffirm the fact. This could become a self-fulfilling prophecy because they are investing vast amounts of money into weapons production.”

articles.title: In Poland, preparations are underway for a possible Russian hybrid attack on the border with Ukraine
articles.body:
In Poland, preparations are underway for a possible Russian hybrid attack on the border with Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
In the border town of Dorohusk, traffic was suspended three times due to the threat of drones or missiles. Warsaw fears new hybrid attacks by Russia.
In the eastern regions of Poland bordering Ukraine, readiness is being strengthened for possible hybrid attacks by Russia involving drones or missiles. Associated Press reports this, UNN writes.
Details
In the border town of Dorohusk, local residents received warnings three times in a single day about a possible drone or missile crossing the border. People were urged to be prepared to take shelter in the event of a threat.
Traffic through the border crossing with Ukraine, located approximately 2 km away, was suspended three times that day. During one of the warnings, checkpoint personnel were even evacuated, while military helicopters flew over the settlement.
Poland fears new Russian attacks
Anxiety in the region intensified after the events of September 13, when two Russian drones exploded on the Ukrainian side of the Dorohusk–Yahodyn crossing. The explosions were clearly heard in Poland.
New anxiety and fear have emerged because those explosions were heard very clearly in our village that night. We had never experienced anything like this before. It was the first time the sirens sounded
On September 17, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia could be preparing hybrid strikes involving drones or missiles against European countries supporting Ukraine. According to him, Polish regions near the Ukrainian border could be particularly vulnerable in the coming months.
Warsaw's concerns relate both to the possible accidental crossing of the border by Russian weapons during attacks on Ukraine and to deliberate provocations. European countries have also previously accused Russia of using other methods of hybrid warfare, including sabotage, cyberattacks, and disinformation.

articles.title: Russia warns UK and NATO of nuclear response over Kaliningrad blockade
articles.body:
Russia warned on Tuesday that any attempt to blockade the Kaliningrad Region by the UK or NATO will be met with a response using all means, including nuclear weapons.
In a statement on Telegram, the Russian Embassy in London said this while responding to UK media reports that discussed the possibility of a NATO blockade of Kaliningrad or non-recognition of Russian sovereignty over the region.
“Those advocating plans to blockade Kaliningrad or launch a strike against it should have no illusions about the consequences. Any military action by the UK or NATO against Russian territory will be met with a response using all means available to Russia, including nuclear weapons,” it stressed.
The embassy reiterated that Russia “does not seek confrontation with NATO and Europe and does not intend to attack them,” adding that those who choose to initiate such a conflict “should not be under any illusions” that Russia would respond accordingly.
Russia will use all means to defend its territory
The Kaliningrad Region is a Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea, situated between Poland and Lithuania and separated from mainland Russia by Lithuanian territory.
Last week, in remarks to Anadolu, the Russian Embassy in Paris also commented on what it described as "provocative statements regarding the possibility of NATO forces striking the Kaliningrad region or blocking access to it."
"We wish to emphasise that Russia will use all means at its disposal to defend its territory and that, should any attempt be made to carry out such plans, the retaliation will be inevitable and overwhelming," the embassy said.

'We will not be intimidated,' Estonian PM says after attributing recent arson attack to Russia
Estonia’s prime minister Kristen Michal does not seem to be convinced by Russia’s denials.
Minutes after we got a response from the Kremlin, he posted on X:
“The arson attack against Milrem Robotics was ordered by Russian special services.
This is part of Russia’s broader campaign across Europe to intimidate us and weaken our support for Ukraine. It will not work.
Our response will be the opposite: stronger security at home, more support for Ukraine and greater pressure on Russia.
We will not be intimidated.”
The Estonian government also published a handy summary of the case so far:
“The criminal investigation into the exact circumstances of the incident is continuing, but the preliminary information gathered so far in the criminal proceedings also indicates that the attack was commissioned. The suspects believed to have directly carried out the arson attack have been apprehended and taken into custody and no longer pose a threat.
On the night of 15 August, a fire broke out in a building used by defence industry company Milrem Robotics on Betooni Street in Tallinn’s Lasnamäe district. Emergency services responded immediately and the fire was quickly brought under control. No lives were in danger.
On 17 August, two Latvian citizens suspected of carrying out the arson attack were detained in Latvia. A third suspect was detained on 18 August. Searches of locations associated with the suspects in Latvia resulted in the seizure of numerous data storage devices and items that may have been used to set fire to the building.
On 17–18 September, Latvia handed over all three suspects to Estonia.”
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.
Estonia said an August arson attack on a drone manufacturer supplying Kyiv was an act of sabotage commissioned by Moscow’s security services (10:10, 10:25), with several allies expressing their solidarity and support for Tallinn (10:20, 10:27, 11:12, 12:46, 13:30).
Estonia’s PM Kristen Michal said the country “will not be intimidated” (12:08)
The Kremlin rejected what it called Estonia’s “baseless” accusation, with spokesperson saying it was “ill considered” and “absolutely no relation to reality” (11:32).
In other news,
Nato secretary general Mark Rutte has urged allies to keep calm and carry on supporting Ukraine, saying Russia is “failing to undermine” the alliance’s support for Kyiv despite growing number of sabotage, drone incidents against Nato(11:07).
Lithuania’s prime minister MindaugasSinkevičius pushed back against recent warnings from Denmark, Poland and Germany about a potential imminent threat, saying there is no evidence of Russia “getting ready” to act against the region (11:10).

Could Burnham's new post-Brexit vision see a move away from Starmer's red lines? - snap analysis
Lisa O’Carroll
Senior correspondent
Andy Burnham’s promise to set out a new vision for the UK’s post Brexit relationship with the EU later this year unleashes the prospects of a dramatic move away from Keir Starmer’s red lies of not rejoining the single market or customs union.
All day yesterday in Liverpool, rumours were swirling that Burnham had some big reveal on the EU in his speech.
Although he didn’t specify what the new relationship would look like, announcing he wants a consultation on options the Labour party can embrace, will be music to ears of people like Stella Creasy, the head of Labour’s movement for Europe group.
“Today the prime minister, Andy Burnham, showed he understands the damage Brexit has done and will lead this country back towards a future with Europe.”
”There’s never been a more important time to join the @labourmovementforeurope to be part of shaping what comes next,” she wrote as he left the hall.
Burnham announced he would be looking at all options for the UK’s post Brexit relationship around the next summit with the EU, due to be held at the end of November.
Although ministers over the weekend including Europe minister Hamish Falconer had insisted Andy Burnham was “ambitious” for his plans with the EU, there was no details of what that looked like. Until today.
Burnham has now raised the prospects that he could blur or even rub out Keir Starmer’s red lines, not joining the single market or customs union, or even go into the next election promising another referendum to rejoin the EU.
Only yesterday Lord Liddle, a Labour grandee, was telling a panel on the EU in Liverpool that the UK had “got rather stuck” in its negotiations with Brussels.
Starmer, he said, could never really make up his mind about where he wanted the UK to be.
He “blew hot and cold” and “the red lines were brought out too often” Liddle said referring to Starmer’s insistence the UK would not rejoin the single market or customs union.
If the UK is serious about group, Liddle said, “the first thing” it has to look at is “the relationship with the EU”.
Burnham to set out 'options' for Britain's EU relationship later this year
In his speech Burnham also talked about his plans to look at Britain’s future relationship with the EU again.
“We will not give Britain the clear path we need into the rest of this century until we decide on a long term relationship with what is still our largest market.
I cannot say to you truthfully that where we are is good enough. Brexit has done more harm than good.
We need to restore a higher level of growth and prosperity for Britain.
So I will take the opportunity around the summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe the different options are for Britain’s long term relationship with our European partners.
And there are different options, and I will see if we can find consensus around one.”
Burnham lays out reforms plans to make Britain 'more resilient to the shocks we will undoubtedly face'
Over in the UK, prime minister Andy Burnham is addressing the Labour party conference this afternoon, setting his plans for the country.
In a brief passage on security and defence, he says:
“A country [reformed] like that will be much more resilient to the shocks we will undoubtedly face in the rest of this century and more able to meet its Nato obligations on defence …
I will be steadfast in my support for Ukraine, and stand up to threats whenever they come from: Russia, Iran, or anywhere.”
If you’re interested in details, my colleague Andrew Sparrow has all of it over on the UK blog:
‘It keeps growing’: the tent camp that stands against Spain’s housing crisis
Ashifa Kassam
in Madrid
Wielding a broom and dustpan, Marta García, 60, darted past the edges of tents, sweeping up bits of litter as she passed a poster that read: “What kind of times are these, when we need to defend the obvious?”
On Saturday, as tens of thousands of people took to the streets of Madrid to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis, the retired schoolteacher was among a small group who had sought to take the protest one step further.
“At first we were 10 tents,” she said, gesturing to the sprawling encampment set up in the central Puerta del Sol plaza behind her. “Now, we’re more than 300 tents, and it keeps growing.”
The shock soon gave way to anger as the octogenarian was shown being brought out of her home on a stretcher, flanked by protesters on one side and police officers on the other.
Housing campaigners seized on the moment. “The whole country has seen that housing speculation has no mercy on anyone,” said Alicia del Río of the Madrid Tenants’ Union. “We’re not sad, we’re angry. And we’re not going to stop until we change things.”
Two former Hungarian ministers detained over suspected bribery and misuse of public funds
Jon Henley
Two ministers in Viktor Orbán’s former far-right government suspected separately of misusing millions of euros of public funds and taking millions more in bribes have been detained, hours after Hungarian MPs voted to lift their immunity.
Prosecutors said on Tuesday that Balázs Hankó, Orbán’s culture minister and still an MP in the former prime minister’s nationalist Fidesz party, was taken into custody late on Monday. Hankó is suspected of misappropriation of funds. He has denied any wrongdoing.
Miklós Seszták, an MP from Fidesz ally KDNP who served as minister for national development between 2014 and 2018, was also detained on Monday as part of an investigation into alleged bribery. He too has denied wrongdoing.
In more US-Russia relationship news, Interfax reports that Russian economy minister Maxim Reshetnikov will take part in a G20 trade ministers’ meeting in the US which is scheduled to start tomorrow.
Russian president Vladimir Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev had meetings with representatives of US departments of Treasury and Energy during his visit to Washington, sources have told Reuters.
It is a further sign of the Trump administration normalising relations with Russia despite the ongoing attacks on Ukraine and concerns over Russia’s action from Nato allies. Last week US secretary of state Marco Rubio said the US had invited Putin to attend a G20 summit scheduled for Miami in December.
Russia's 'terror against Ukraine' is 'intensifying by the day,' Ukraine's foreign minister warns
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha condemned Russia’s “terror against Ukraine” which he says is “intensifying by the day,” after another night of attacks on Kyiv and Odesa region.
“This is Russia’s deliberate escalation instead of accepting Ukraine’s offers to cease fire, negotiate, and end the war. Putin’s rejection of peace must have consequences for Russia,” Sybiha said.
He said:
“We are grateful to all partners who are strengthening Ukraine’s air defence and providing the systems and interceptors that are saving lives right now. Every successful interception proves that this support works.
At the same time, Russia must face growing pressure for every new wave of terror. Stronger sanctions, fewer resources for its war machine, and fewer opportunities to circumvent existing restrictions.
Moscow should not be allowed to turn another winter into a weapon. Every Russian escalation must bring the opposite of what the Kremlin expects – stronger protection for Ukraine, greater pressure on Russia, and a higher price for continuing this war.”

articles.title: Zelensky, Jewish community leaders commemorate 85th anniversary of Nazi's Babyn Yar WWII massacre
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky attended an annual memorial ceremony to commemorate the tens of thousands of Jews massacred by Nazis at Babyn Yar on Tuesday, which happened 85 years ago on September 29 and 30, 1941.
Several Jewish Ukrainian leaders, including those from the Chabad community, were present at the event. The ceremony was organized by Ukraine's Presidential Office, the Babyn Yar memorial complex, and the Federation of Jewish Communities of Ukraine.
"We must remember the terrible things that happened here many years ago, and now they are happening again, this time at the hands of the Russians," Zelensky said.
"Thank you very much for being with us here today, and thank you for praying for Ukraine, for Ukrainians, for all those who have been killed in Ukraine, for the tragic moments we have endured, and for the Jews who were tortured and murdered. Never again!" Zelensky stated.
Representatives from about 50 countries attended, including Israel's Ambassador to Ukraine Roi Rosenblit. Zelensky thanked the ambassadors and the international community for their "help in fighting against the terrible things the Russians are doing to us, to humanity, and to civilization."
Ukrainian security forces deployed special air-defense systems and snipers positioned around the site due to concerns over a possible attack, particularly threats posed by Russian drones.
Zelensky discusses arrangements for remains of Israeli teen killed in Kyiv to be returned to Israel
While attending, Zelensky discussed Daniel Umansky, an Israeli child who was killed by a Russian drone strike in Kyiv last week, with the FJCU, particularly regarding the arrangements to transport his remains to Israel for burial.
One of the attendees, who has been running Jewish community and educational institutions in Kyiv for nearly 30 years, discussed her grandmother, who was murdered in Babyn Yar.
"Grandmother Sonia was murdered in her fifties. We were unable to find a photograph of her, but we recently located a testimony at Yad Vashem containing her details," Rebbetzin Devorah Leah Levenhartz said.
"It turns out that before her murder, she lived not far from where we ourselves lived, and she now gets to be part of the thriving Jewish community we established...It is almost impossible to comprehend," she added.
"The tragedy of Babyn Yar is an absolutely tragic and bloody example, and today we are meeting on the 85th anniversary of the tragedy of Babyn Yar," Zelensky said in his address.
"This tragedy reminds us how painful it is to lose our family and loved ones, and how the value of human life can be diminished," he added.
"I want to thank you for understanding the value of life. That is, of course, felt especially strongly in Ukraine during this shameful, unprovoked war by Russia against Ukraine, against society, against people, and against life itself," he continued.
What happened in the Babyn Yar Massacre?
On September 29-30, 1941, the Nazis gunned down nearly 34,000 Jews in Babyn Yar in what would later be considered the first massacre of the Jews in the Holocaust.
Babyn Yar is located near Kyiv, which the Nazis took control of on September 19, 1941. A few days later, there was a large explosion at the German command post that killed many German soldiers. The Nazis blamed the explosion on the Jews, intensifying their hatred, so when the SS troops entered Kyiv, the city's Jews were immediately marked for destruction.
Between September 29 and 30, nearly 34,000 Jewish men, women, and children were marched to the ravine of Babyn Yar, stripped and machine-gunned into a mass grave, which was immediately covered, burying some of the victims alive.
The grave was filled with thousands more bodies over the next two years. The total is unclear, but at least 100,000 people were murdered at Babyn Yar over two years. The victims were primarily Jewish, but they also included communists, Soviet prisoners of war, and Roma people.
Despite the tragedy that occurred at Babyn Yar, it took the Soviet Union 25 years to acknowledge the massacre. After trying unsuccessfully to build a sports stadium over the mass grave in 1961, the Soviet Union constructed a small obelisk to stand at the site.
In 1974, a 15-meter memorial statue was erected, but still, there was no hint of the fact that Jews had been murdered at Babyn Yar, as the identification of the victims was vague and did not mention the word 'Jew.'
Only in 1991, 50 years after the massacre, when Ukraine declared independence, was the identity of the victims properly recorded on the memorial, recognizing the massacre of Jews at the site.
Ariella Marsden contributed to this report.

articles.title: Honeywell gets $25.6M for nuclear-tough navigation gyro
articles.body:
- The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory awarded Honeywell $25.6 million to mature a compact, radiation-hardened strategic gyroscope, with work due by July 2029.
- The contract follows a $41.6 million laboratory award in 2020 for Honeywell to design a Compact Strategic-Grade Gyroscope.
The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory has awarded Honeywell Aerospace $25.6 million to keep developing a small, radiation-hardened gyroscope accurate enough for “strategic” use, the class of navigation sensor that has to work in space and survive the effects of a nuclear environment.
The cost-plus-fixed-fee contract covers what the Pentagon calls the compact strategic gyroscope maturation project, the U.S. Department of War said. Honeywell will do the work in Clearwater, Florida, and is expected to finish by July 1, 2029. The laboratory’s office at Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico, is managing the contract.
Combined with accelerometers in an inertial navigation system, it lets a missile, satellite, ship or aircraft work out where it is and which way it is pointing without GPS or any other outside signal. “Strategic-grade” refers to the most accurate class of these sensors, used where drift has to stay extremely low for long periods, such as in ballistic missile guidance and satellite pointing. Radiation hardening means the sensor and its electronics are built to keep working when hit by the radiation found in space or produced by a nuclear blast.
The notice does not say which weapon or spacecraft the gyroscope is intended for.
The award builds on earlier Air Force Research Laboratory work with the same company. In early 2020, the laboratory’s Space Vehicles Directorate at Kirtland gave Honeywell a $41.6 million contract to design a Compact Strategic-Grade Gyroscope, Military & Aerospace Electronics reported. That five-year effort, carried out at Honeywell’s Phoenix site, called for building and testing four prototypes, refining the design into six strategic-grade units, developing a radiation-hardened custom chip and software for the gyro, flying it on an experimental satellite for a one-year mission in low Earth orbit, and laying out a path toward a gyroscope that could keep operating through the radiation and electromagnetic pulse of nuclear explosions. The earlier contract was scheduled to run through August 2025.
The Department of War did not say how much of the first project’s goals were met or whether the space flight took place. The new work is described as “maturation,” which in defense research usually means taking a design that has been shown to work and making it more reliable, easier to build and closer to use in a real system.
The contract was competitively awarded, and the government received two offers. Only $500,000 in fiscal 2026 research and development money was committed at the time of award, with the rest of the $25.6 million to be added in later years.
Honeywell’s Clearwater site is one of the company’s main centers for navigation and inertial sensor work. The notice did not name the second bidder.

articles.title: Russian nuclear-capable Tu-95 crashes in Far East, killing six crew members
articles.body:
The bomber went down near Krasnoyarovo shortly after taking off from the Ukrainka air base, which Russia had used to shelter surviving strategic bombers after Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb destroyed or damaged more than 40 aircraft at Russian airfields in June 2025.
A Russian military plane crashed in the far eastern region of Amur on Tuesday, killing six crew members and leaving another injured, the Russian defence ministry said.
The Russian defence ministry said the military aircraft went down in an uninhabited area during a training flight and was not carrying ammunition.
"According to preliminary data, six crew members died, while one was injured and evacuated to a medical facility," the ministry added.
According to the Russian state-affiliated media, the crash occurred near the village of Krasnoyarovo shortly after the bomber took off from the Ukrainka air base.
Authorities have opened a criminal case and an investigative commission from Russia's Aerospace Forces has been flown to the crash site. Initial assessments suggest the aircraft went down because of a technical malfunction.
Unverified videos posted on social media showed what appeared to be flames and smoke rising from the crash site, with booming and crackling sounds in the background.
The Tu-95 is a large, nuclear-capable bomber designed in the Soviet Union, first flown in 1952. It is the only turboprop-powered strategic bomber still in operational use.
The Ukrainka air base — one of Russia's largest strategic long-range bases — is located in the Seryshevo district of the Amur region, in the country's Far East.
In June 2025, it was among the targets of a major operation by Ukraine's security service SBU against Russian military airfields codenamed Spiderweb.
In Operation Spiderweb, FPV drones concealed in lorries with remotely opening roofs were used to destroy or damage more than 40 Russian aircraft, including between seven and eight Tu-95s.
Russia redeployed the surviving strategic bombers from its European air bases to Ukrainka.

articles.title: British warship hits frigate with live Naval Strike Missile
articles.body:
The Royal Navy used both of its newest anti-ship missiles during a joint US-UK live-fire exercise off the Hebrides that ended with the sinking of the decommissioned American frigate USS Klakring, firing the Naval Strike Missile from HMS Portland and Sea Venom from a Wildcat helicopter of 815 Naval Air Squadron operating from her flight deck.
The round Portland fired carried a warhead and was aimed at a real ship rather than a range target, which the service describes as the first Royal Navy firing of a Naval Strike Missile, although HMS Somerset launched one off Norway in September last year.
Lieutenant Commander Louise Kirkaldy, HMS Portland’s principal warfare officer, said: “The successful firing of Naval Strike Missile marks a significant milestone for the Royal Navy, demonstrating our ability to deliver credible, modern maritime strike capability. This achievement reflects the professionalism, dedication and teamwork of all those involved, whose hard work has ensured we remain ready to meet the challenges of today and tomorrow.”
Petty Officer James Kenyon, an above water warfare specialist aboard the frigate, fired it. “To be involved in such a high-profile exercise is the highlight of my career,” he said. “Being the first person to fire war-shot Naval Strike Missile and achieve a hit is a very proud moment, and one that will stay with me for the rest of my career. This was the culmination of over a year’s effort in planning and bringing the drills into service, and I am glad that I was able to contribute.”
Commander Dafydd Bryden, the ship’s commanding officer, said: “The opportunity to fire anti-ship missiles against a decommissioned warship is an important test of our warfighting capability. This engagement proved the effectiveness of these systems as well as the sailors and aircrew who operate them. We remain ready to fight and win at sea.”
Sea Venom was fired from the Wildcat during the same serial, and Captain Kelechi Ndukwe, commander of Task Force 65, confirmed to journalists that it was the missile’s first live firing since reaching initial operating capability, and that it hit the target. According to the Royal Navy, the helicopter completed the full kill chain by detecting, identifying and striking the target rather than simply releasing the weapon.
Lieutenant Commander Rhydian Edwards, test and evaluation commander at the Maritime Aviation Strike Operational Advantage Group, said: “This was a landmark moment for the Wildcat Force. For the first time we demonstrated the live firing of an operational Sea Venom missile against a representative maritime target. More importantly, we proved our ability to execute the full maritime strike kill chain under realistic operational conditions.
“This was about giving commanders confidence that Wildcat can find, fix and strike maritime targets using Sea Venom as part of a wider task group. The lessons learned from this activity will directly inform future tactics, training and operational capability development, ensuring Maritime Aviation Strike remains ready to fight and win when called upon.”
The Naval Strike Missile was brought into Royal Navy service under an interim arrangement to replace Harpoon, which left service in 2023, and has been fitted to Type 23 frigates and Type 45 destroyers using equipment transferred between hulls as ships enter and leave refit. Built by Kongsberg, the weapon is a sea-skimming missile with a low radar signature and a range well beyond that of the system it replaced, and it can strike land targets as well as ships. The service says it carries an advanced warhead, travels close to supersonic speeds and can reach targets more than 100 miles away while evading detection by skimming the sea, and that it will be complementary to the Future Cruise Anti-Ship Weapon, intended to become the fleet’s premier long-range anti-ship missile aboard the Type 26 and Type 31 frigates through the Mk41 vertical launch system.
Sea Venom, built by MBDA, is the Wildcat’s principal anti-ship weapon and replaced the Sea Skua carried by the Lynx. The Royal Navy describes it as designed to defeat corvette sized vessels or disable frigates, destroyers and other larger ships, with a Wildcat able to carry four at once, and says it can also be used overland against bunkers, buildings and vehicles. Readers will have seen the same missile turn up this week on a very different platform, fitted by STARK to an uncrewed surface vessel built near Plymouth.
The two British weapons were part of a wider engagement in which USS Paul Ignatius demonstrated the maximum damage and range capability of an anti-surface variant of the Standard Missile 6, and the submarine USS Massachusetts engaged the target with the Mark 48 Advanced Capability Torpedo, which delivered the final hit and sank the ship, as we reported.
Weapons were used in order of reach too we understand, with the longest range ordnance going first. Ndukwe said the American side started with the SM-6 before moving in to shorter range systems, a sequence designed to get the most out of the sensors fitted to the hull for battle damage assessment.
Atlantic Thunder 2026 was led by United States Sixth Fleet and drew in forces from five American task forces alongside the Royal Navy, the Royal Air Force and the United States Air Force. Lieutenant Commander Paul Atkins, the United Kingdom lead project officer for the exercise, said: “Atlantic Thunder 26 demonstrated the enduring strength of the UK-US alliance and the close partnership between the Royal Navy and the United States Navy. Operating together in a demanding environment, we showcased our ability to integrate seamlessly, share expertise and deliver a highly capable, interoperable maritime force. Through combined training and operations, we have strengthened our collective warfighting capability, reinforcing our ability to deter potential adversaries and deliver maritime combat power whenever and wherever it is required.”

articles.title: Why is South Korea so angry with Ukraine over two North Korean prisoners of war?
articles.body:
South Korea and Ukraine are locked in an escalating diplomatic dispute over who agreed what regarding the circumstances of two prisoners of war captured fighting for Russia.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, told the UN general assembly last week that his country had “sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea”.
Seoul had long said it would take the men. But rather than celebrate, on Monday South Korea summoned Ukraine’s most senior diplomat in Seoul and demanded an apology.
Here’s a brief guide to what has happened, and why.
Who are the PoWs and what has happened to them?
Ukrainian forces captured the two men in Russia’s Kursk region in January 2025. They were among thousands of troops Pyongyang sent to fight for Moscow. Both men later said they wanted to go to South Korea, which regards North Koreans as its own citizens.
In July, Zelenskyy and South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, agreed to resolve the issue while respecting the soldiers’ “free will”. The captured pair reportedly arrived in South Korea via a third country earlier this month.
North Koreans arriving in the South as defectors are usually questioned by the National Intelligence Service before being sent to a state resettlement centre, although sensitive cases can reportedly bypass the centre.
Why is Seoul so angry?
Seoul says Kyiv requested secrecy about the transfer, fearing domestic criticism for passing up the opportunity to exchange them for “a large number” of Ukrainian prisoners. South Korea says it agreed, citing the safety of the two men and their families as well as diplomatic and security considerations.
After Zelenskyy revealed the transfer in his UN speech, Lee said on X that Ukraine had broken a “non-disclosure agreement” and that this was regrettable. Zelenskyy’s adviser Dmytro Lytvyn responded on Facebook that there had been no such agreement, prompting accusations from Lee’s critics that the president, whose approval rating has hit a low of 37.9%, had lied.
Lee’s office called Kyiv’s statement “false” and said its conduct “seriously damages trust” between the two governments. On Monday, the foreign ministry summoned Ukraine’s chargé d’affaires, demanding an apology at governmental level.
Was there actually an agreement?
South Korea’s foreign ministry told Ukraine’s envoy there had been a “clear agreement”. Asked by the Guardian the same day whether anything had been put in writing, the ministry said only that the two sides “had decided to handle it confidentially”. Ukraine’s embassy in Seoul did not respond to a request for comment.
Has North Korea said anything?
No. South Korea’s unification ministry said it had “not identified any related developments so far” and would continue monitoring.
North Korea has glorified soldiers who killed themselves rather than be captured. The transfer of two who survived and chose the South is “a fatal matter” for Pyongyang, says Cho Han-bum of the Korea Institute for National Unification. Having built a “heroic narrative” around its troops, the regime is unlikely to disclose the transfer domestically, he says.
How big a diplomatic incident is this?
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, South Korea condemned Moscow’s actions, joined western sanctions and, in July, pledged a $100m support package. But it has kept the war at arm’s length, refusing to send weapons directly to Kyiv, in line with its practice of not supplying lethal arms to countries at war. Before the war, Russia was one of South Korea’s biggest trading partners. Lee’s government is also keen to improve relations with Pyongyang.
The row has turned that cautious support for Kyiv into open criticism, largely from Lee’s own camp. Kim Byung-joo, a Democratic party lawmaker, said there was “no reason or need” to support Ukraine and has urged the government to review its aid “immediately”.

articles.title: Araghchi’s diplomacy in NY puts war, Hormuz and nuclear rights at center of Iran’s UN outreach
articles.body:
Araghchi’s diplomacy in NY puts war, Hormuz and nuclear rights at center of Iran’s UN outreach
TEHRAN- Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has concluded an intensive round of diplomatic consultations in New York, using the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly to press Iran’s positions on the war, the Strait of Hormuz, the nuclear issue, international law and the continuation of diplomacy.
Araghchi left New York for Tehran early Tuesday after several days of bilateral and multilateral meetings with foreign ministers, senior officials, United Nations representatives, international organizations, think tanks and media outlets. He also accompanied President Masoud Pezeshkian during parts of the Iranian delegation’s intensive UNGA program.
 
 The diplomatic activity came against the backdrop of the ongoing confrontation between Iran and the United States and Israel, with Tehran seeking to place its account of the conflict, its security concerns and its conditions for a diplomatic settlement before the international community.
Diplomacy amid war
In his assessment of the New York mission, Araghchi said one of Iran’s principal objectives had been to ensure that the Iranian people’s legitimate grievances and suffering were heard internationally, while defending the country’s national interests and demonstrating that Iran remained an active and confident participant in international diplomacy.
He said the large number of meetings requested by other governments demonstrated that Iran had not become diplomatically isolated. Araghchi said many countries had expressed an interest in engaging with Iran and that the meetings provided an opportunity to discuss both bilateral issues and the wider regional crisis.
A central element of the Iranian diplomatic message was the war and its consequences for regional security, particularly the situation surrounding the Strait of Hormuz. Araghchi said Iran had made a deliberate effort to explain its position on the strategic waterway to both the United States and the wider international community.
Hormuz becomes the immediate diplomatic issue
The Strait of Hormuz emerged as the most immediate issue in Araghchi’s consultations.
According to the Iranian foreign minister, Tehran has presented conditions that must be fulfilled before the waterway can be reopened. He described those conditions as fair and reasonable, arguing that if Washington genuinely seeks a negotiated and peaceful solution, Iran has already presented a framework for achieving one.
Araghchi said Iran’s seven-point proposal had been transmitted to Washington through Qatari mediation. Following a fresh meeting with a Qatari mediator in New York, the two sides discussed ideas for meeting Iran’s conditions, with the mediator expected to relay those ideas to the US side and convey Washington’s response back to Tehran.
Araghchi said he expected the process to produce a response soon, while making clear that any subsequent decision would be taken in Tehran. He also stressed that communication through Qatari and Pakistani intermediaries had existed previously but had become more substantive following Iran’s latest proposal.
The significance of the Hormuz issue extends beyond maritime navigation in Tehran’s presentation of the crisis. Iran has linked the reopening of the waterway to broader security conditions, arguing that the issue cannot be separated from the country’s national security and the wider confrontation with Washington.
That position was reiterated by Araghchi after reports emerged suggesting that Tehran might have modified its conditions. He categorically rejected that interpretation, saying there had been “no change” in Iran’s position and that the conditions for reopening the Strait remained clear. He said the immediate issue under discussion was Hormuz and warned against deliberate media speculation about Iranian flexibility.
Tehran presses UN over violations
One of Araghchi’s most consequential meetings was with UN Secretary-General António Guterres on the final day of his New York visit.
Araghchi briefed Guterres on developments in West Asia following US-Israeli military aggression, and criticized the United Nations’ failure to respond adequately to violations of the UN Charter and international law.
He argued that Iran, as a founding member of the United Nations, expected the organization and its member states to respond to blatant breaches of international law, particularly actions involving a permanent member of the Security Council. He called for an explicit condemnation of Washington’s interventionist measures and threats against Iran.
Araghchi also referred to two rounds of US and Israeli attacks on Iran during negotiations in less than a year, as well as the continuation of a naval blockade and “economic terrorism.”
He stressed that Iran would continue to pursue accountability for those responsible for war crimes.
The meeting also covered Iran’s complaint regarding restrictions imposed by the United States on the normal activities of Iran’s UN mission. Araghchi called on the UN Secretary-General to take steps to ensure Washington meets its obligations under the UN Headquarters Agreement.
Nuclear issue remains part of Tehran’s broader diplomatic message
While Hormuz was presented as the immediate issue in the latest mediation effort, Araghchi also reiterated Iran’s positions on its nuclear program and its national rights.
In his meetings during the UNGA, the foreign minister linked the nuclear issue to the broader question of Iran’s rights, national sovereignty and the future of diplomacy. The Iranian delegation’s approach was therefore not limited to seeking a temporary arrangement over maritime traffic but sought to frame any diplomatic process within a wider set of security and political concerns.
This distinction is important in understanding Tehran’s position: Iranian officials have continued to emphasize that diplomacy remains available, while arguing that negotiations must address the consequences of military action, economic pressure and violations of Iran’s sovereign rights.
Outreach to Russia and the Global South
Araghchi’s New York diplomacy also extended beyond the immediate Iran-US dispute.
The Iranian foreign minister held talks with Mali’s Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop, where he emphasized Tehran’s interest in strengthening relations with developing countries, particularly African states and members of the Alliance of Sahel States.
Araghchi expressed Iran’s readiness to hold a joint meeting with the three members of the Sahel alliance and reiterated Tehran’s stated support for the independence and national sovereignty of developing countries. He also criticized European interference in the internal affairs of Sahel states.
A similar message emerged from his meeting with Nigerien Foreign Minister Bakary Yaou Sangaré. Araghchi welcomed Niger’s position against the politicized or instrumental use of the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Board of Governors against Iran and discussed expanding bilateral relations and cooperation within the Sahel alliance framework.
Araghchi also met Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath on the sidelines of the UNGA, as part of a broader series of talks with counterparts from different regions.
A diplomatic message shaped by confrontation
Taken together, Araghchi’s New York meetings reflected an Iranian diplomatic strategy built around three interconnected messages: Tehran says it remains open to diplomacy; it rejects negotiations under coercive conditions; and it intends to link any progress toward de-escalation to concrete security and political arrangements.
The seven-point proposal transmitted through Qatar represents the most immediate channel for testing whether that approach can produce movement, with Tehran awaiting Washington’s response through the mediators. At the same time, Araghchi’s meetings at the United Nations demonstrate that Iran is pursuing a broader diplomatic campaign over the war, international law, the nuclear issue, sanctions and regional security.
For an Iranian diplomatic delegation attending a UN General Assembly held amid an ongoing military confrontation, the New York mission therefore served two purposes simultaneously: defending Iran’s position before the international community and keeping channels for a negotiated settlement open.
Araghchi’s departure from New York does not mark the end of that process. As he emphasized before leaving, the channels through Qatar and other mediators remain available, and any response from Washington is expected to be assessed by Tehran before Iran determines its next step.

articles.title: Lavrov accuses Europe of waging war on Russia
articles.body:
Elena Teslova
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
European countries are waging a war against Russia, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Tuesday.
Speaking on the sidelines of the of the Valdai forum in Moscow, Lavrov said European countries are supplying weapons to Ukraine that are being used against Russia.
“This is a war that Europe is waging against us,” Lavrov said, rejecting European accusations that Russia’s strikes on cargo vessels carrying Western weapons to Ukraine amounted to a “hybrid covert war” by Moscow.
Russia's use of force in Ukraine, he said, was strictly self-defense to elimintate threats.
“If you mean the destruction of infrastructure that is being used by the Nazi regime, with Western support, to wage war against the Russian Federation, then we are using force to suppress this direct threat to us,” he said.
US-Russia talks
On plans for talks with the US, he said they will take place soon.
“We agreed with (US Secretary of State) Marco Rubio that this will happen. Experts should coordinate the specific dates and the specific place,” he noted.
Lavrov cited the return of Russian diplomatic property seized by the US as one of the outstanding issues in Moscow-Washington relations.
According to him, Russia received no encouraging signals from the administration of US President Donald Trump regarding its return.
“There have never been any encouraging comments from the Americans, already under the administration of Donald Trump, on this issue,” he said.
Lavrov acknowledged that the US is still seeking to advance its unilateral interests, but said Washington is nevertheless forced to engage with countries including Russia and China.
Berlin scared of 'missing the train'
Commenting on Poland’s plans to produce Patriot missiles and Europe’s involvement in the Ukraine conflict, Lavrov urged European countries to study Russia’s military doctrine.
Turning to his meeting with the German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul’s on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, Lavrov said Berlin may be seeking to become involved in efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict because it does not want to “miss the train.”
“It is difficult for me to judge what Germany is seeking. I think one explanation that is obvious is simply the desire not to miss the train. They believe the train has already gained momentum — I don't know if that's true, it's hard for me to judge, if they mean the Ukrainian crisis,” he said.
Asked about the agenda for his meeting with Wadephul, Lavrov said the German minister spoke about the “militarization of the European Union,” continued calls for NATO to expand and admit Ukraine, and claims that “Russia is an eternal enemy” and that “in three years we will be at war.”
“If such incantations are being voiced, and the goal, as Mr. Wadephul himself announced it, is simply to reproduce these incantations behind closed doors, without the press, so that Russia supposedly understands that this is all really the case — then this is a futile, and I would even say harmful, undertaking,” he said.
Lavrov said it was “very sad” that some EU and NATO officials were effectively acting as “spokesmen” for what he described as the European position.

articles.title: Russia wants Iran to remain part of nuclear treaty: Kremlin
articles.body:
Burc Eruygur
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
Russia on Tuesday urged Iran to remain 'a responsible party' to the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) following statements from Tehran that it seeks to withdraw from the nuclear treaty.
 
Speaking to reporters during a press briefing, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow has heard statements on the possibility of Tehran’s withdrawal from the NPT from Ali Nikzad, the Iranian parliament’s deputy speaker, and that these remarks require further clarification.
 
“We would not want Iran to withdraw from the NPT. We consider the NPT to be the cornerstone of the non-proliferation regime. And we do hope that Iran will remain an important and responsible party to this treaty,” Peskov said.
 
The spokesman’s remarks come as Iranian media outlets, including the state-run broadcaster IRIB, reported Monday that Nikzad said the country’s parliament will review a “triple-urgency” motion to withdraw from the NPT.
 
According to reports, Nikzad stated that Tehran, which became a party to the treaty in March 1970, has no trust in the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), or IAEA chief Rafael Grossi, because he conducts “merely superficial inspections and submits negative reports against Iran.”
 
He was further quoted as saying that the motion is currently under review and will be deliberated on the very same day it is formally tabled, adding that the parliament will also examine the international implications of the move.
 
Commenting on the Ukraine war, Peskov said that Moscow sees "no voices of reason" calling for dialogue or for rectifying the situation with Russia in the West.
 
"This makes it necessary to consistently pursue the 'special military operation' in order to fully -- one hundred percent -- safeguard our national interests," Peskov said.
 
He also said that a presidential decree on introducing temporary management at Western companies operating in Russia is not aimed at changing ownership, but rather about introducing external management.
 
Noting that the process is reversible, Peskov said that the growing involvement of "unfriendly" countries in "direct combat operations" against Russia was taken into account amid its introduction. "However, we do not currently see any prerequisites for such a reversal," he added.
 
Peskov further dismissed statements by Estonia accusing Russia of being involved in an arson attack on a building used by the Milrem Robotics defense company in the country's capital Tallinn last month as "baseless, ill-considered," and said they "have absolutely no relation to reality, and lack any form of reasoning."

articles.title: Mavic vs Slavic: Ukrainian developers adapt reconnaissance drones to the modern battlefield
articles.body:
Ukrainian company Vyriy Industries is bringing a new tactical reconnaissance drone, Slavic, to the market, Oboronka reports, citing information from the manufacturer. The control system of the new drone will be familiar to DJI Mavic operators, the company also said.
Mavic has long been one of the main reconnaissance tools used by Ukrainian forces, with Ukraine relying heavily on supplies of these drones from abroad. After Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said China had stopped selling drones to Ukraine, the country began seeking alternatives. Slavic is one of these domestic alternatives, designed not only to replace Mavic but also to adapt its capabilities to current battlefield conditions, allowing reconnaissance crews to operate farther from the line of contact and reducing risks to personnel.
Slavic has a tactical range of up to 30 kilometers without GPS
Slavic can remain airborne for up to 1.5 hours because it is equipped with a 40,000 mAh solid-state battery, the media outlet notes. The drone has a tactical range of up to 30 kilometers, the report says.
The aircraft can operate without GPS, as Slavic uses optical positioning for navigation. The pilot can also select a less congested channel and operate more effectively in difficult terrain because the communications system operates across a wide range of channels.
The manufacturer notes that for surveillance, Slavic is equipped with a daytime 2K digital camera mounted on a three-axis stabilized gimbal, with 10x optical and 30x hybrid zoom.
The system is supplied as a ready-to-use package “out of the box,” with all the equipment needed for operation without additional field modifications.
The drone is designed to keep crews farther from the front line
The company said its new drone has successfully completed initial combat trials with seven units of the Ukrainian Defense Forces and is preparing for scale-up, the media outlet notes.
“The war has changed, and so have the working conditions for crews. The kill zone has expanded, while available commercial drones have a limited tactical range. The main task now is to provide the military with a specialized platform that can fly longer and farther, so crews can operate farther from the line of contact. This is exactly why we began developing Slavic,” said Oleksii Babenko, founder and CEO of Vyriy Industries.
At the same time, the team is working on new Slavic configurations, including testing thermal imaging modules for nighttime reconnaissance. The manufacturer is also preparing the platform for scaled-up production and deliveries to the Ukrainian Defense Forces, the company told the media.
“Frankensteins” and Ukrainian-made drones are among the options for replacing scarce Mavics
The Ukrainian military had widely used Chinese DJI Mavic 3 drones, including to adjust artillery fire, monitor infantry positions and conduct surveillance, prompting Ukraine to seek ways to replace the shortage. More than five alternatives to the Chinese drone had already been developed in Ukraine, the Ministry of Strategic Industries of Ukraine confirmed to RBC-Ukraine in July 2025.
There are also other options for replacing them. The main work in military units is being done with “Frankensteins,” drones assembled from two or three damaged aircraft, Mavic UAV pilot instructor “Dobryi” said in an interview with Militarnyi in July this year. At the same time, such drones are less reliable than new ones, he added.

articles.title: Raytheon expands Sidewinder supplier base in U.S., Europe
articles.body:
The U.S. Navy is paying Raytheon up to $30.2 million to line up additional suppliers for key parts of the AIM-9X Sidewinder air-to-air missile, including the cooling engine for its heat-seeking sensor and its warhead components.
The undefinitized contract modification, announced by the U.S. Department of War, covers engineering work to qualify new manufacturing sources for several AIM-9X components. Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, awarded it without competition, and the work is due to be finished in February 2030.
Qualifying a second source means testing and approving another factory to make a part that currently comes from only one supplier, so that production does not stop if that supplier falls behind or shuts down. The notice lists the parts involved: the cryoengine, which cools the missile’s infrared seeker so it can detect a target’s heat; connectors and wiring harnesses; sensor platform and warhead components; components of the optical target detector, which senses when the missile is close enough to its target to detonate; and parts of the inertial measurement unit, which tracks the missile’s movement in flight.
The work will be spread across the United States and Europe. About half, 51%, will take place at Raytheon’s missile plant in Tucson, Arizona. Another 19% is set for Schrobenhausen, Germany, 12% for Anaheim, California, and 8% for Heilbronn, Germany, with smaller shares in Camarillo, California; Delémont, Switzerland; Midland, Ontario; and Logan, Utah.
The modification is a cost-plus-incentive-fee arrangement, meaning the government covers Raytheon’s costs and pays a fee that depends on performance. Because it is undefinitized, work can begin before final prices and terms are agreed, up to a $30.2 million ceiling. The Navy committed $29.6 million in fiscal 2025 weapons procurement funds at the time of award.
The AIM-9X is the latest version of the Sidewinder, a short-range, heat-seeking missile carried by U.S. and allied fighter jets and also fired from the ground by the NASAMS air defense system. The U.S. Navy leads the program jointly with the U.S. Air Force, and more than 35 allied and partner nations use the missile.
In June 2026, the U.S. Navy awarded Raytheon a $1.1 billion contract for more than 1,900 AIM-9X Block II missiles, including 1,653 for U.S. inventories and 336 for foreign customers, with work running through September 2029. That followed another $1.1 billion AIM-9X award in June 2025, then the largest in the program’s history. Raytheon says it is raising AIM-9X production capacity to about 2,500 missiles a year.

articles.title: Estonia slams Russian 'sabotage' after arson attack on defence company Milrem Robotics
articles.body:
European countries have already faced multiple incursions by Russian drones as well as a campaign of covert Russian disruption which began after Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.
NATO chief Mark Rutte urged "calm" on Tuesday over Russia's campaign of sabotage in Europe, saying it was failing to undercut support for Ukraine.
His comments come after Estonia became the latest country to officially blame Russia for such an incident, saying Moscow's "special services" had ordered an arson attack on a defence firm in August.
"Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against NATO allies. It is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine. But Russia is failing. It is failing on the battlefield in Ukraine and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine," Rutte told journalists.
European governments say Moscow is stepping up a campaign of sabotage and interference against Ukraine's backers as the Kremlin's troops struggle on the front line there, more than four years after their February 2022 invasion.
The Estonian incident came just after the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at an airport in Russia that Berlin pinned on Moscow.
Rutte admitted that Russia's activities "can have an impact and sometimes they have an impact, clearly."
But he urged NATO countries to remain "calm, carry on and support Ukraine."
"We should not be naive... about Russia, but they know we are stronger," Rutte said.
Speaking alongside the NATO chief, Lithuania's Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius said intelligence services had no proof Moscow was imminently prepping for something bigger.
"It's a must to say if a threat is there for society, but you can't exaggerate and say something is happening in the upcoming months or weeks," he said.
"The risk remains, but it's not fluctuating...not increasing or decreasing."
Earlier on Tuesday, Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna accused Russia of "sabotage" following an arson attack on the premises of defence company, Milrem Robotics, in August.
"We can conclude with certainty that the arson attack...in Tallinn was an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation," he wrote in a post on X.
He added that the perpetrators of the attack had been apprehended and "no longer pose a threat" and that Estonia had summoned the Russian ambassador.
"This act of sabotage is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe, aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine," Tsahkna wrote.
Estonia, an EU and NATO member state along the alliance's eastern flank, has accused Russia of several "hybrid" provocations since the beginning of Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Along with its neighbours, Latvia and Lithuania, it has ramped up its investment in defence in the years since and remains a staunch ally of Kyiv.
News of the attack prompted messages of solidarity from across Europe.
Germany’s Foreign Minister Johan Wadephul slammed what he called “Russia’s reckless act of hostility and said Estonia had full solidarity from Berlin.
French President Emmanuel Macron said in a post on X that "Russia must know that it will not prevail over either our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine."
"The proliferation of these hostile acts reflects a dangerous escalation on the part of Russia, which will only lead it into a dead end," he added.
Sweden’s Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson called the attack “extremely serious.”
“This pattern of attacks is directed against Europe as a whole. The aim is to weaken our support for Ukraine and to intimidate us. It will not work,” he said in a post on X.
And the European Union said it stands by member state Estonia following the "reckless" arson attack and would not be put off supporting Ukraine.
"We stand by Estonia on this reckless attack," European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand said, expressing "full solidarity" with Tallin.
"Moscow is trying to scare Europe into winding down its support for Ukraine. This will not happen," he added.
The Kremlin rejected what it called Estonia's "baseless" accusation that Russia ordered the arson attack in Tallinn.
"Such statements are baseless, ill-considered, have absolutely no relation to reality and lack any form of reasoning. Consequently, we cannot and will not take such statements seriously," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
Putin trying to break NATO support for Ukraine, leaders say
Putin, Stringer said, is “looking at a whole number of things” to try to create division between NATO allies because his campaign in Ukraine is going badly.
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal likened the Russian leader to a “rat in the corner," who is escalating activity in Europe in an attempt to break Western support for Kyiv at a time when Moscow is under pressure.
Putin is trying to undermine NATO’s collective defence pact by testing nations with covert attacks that are hard to attribute, Michal said.
But the Estonian leader said it's currently “improbable,” that Putin will launch a conventional military attack on Europe because of the threat of a NATO response and because his forces are tied down in Ukraine.
The high level of malign activity from Russia is “here to stay” until Putin changes his military goals, Michal said, adding that the best way to deter him is to “back Ukraine.”

articles.title: The Atlantic: Trump backs plan to ease Russia sanctions in exchange for political prisoners without waiting for the Ukraine war to end
articles.body:
The Atlantic: Trump backs plan to ease Russia sanctions in exchange for political prisoners without waiting for the Ukraine war to end
U.S. President Donald Trump has approved a proposal to ease sanctions on Russia in exchange for the release of political prisoners, The Atlantic reports.
According to the magazine’s Simon Shuster, special envoy John Coale proposed the approach. Coale secured the release of about 500 political prisoners in Belarus in exchange for sanctions relief.
Washington and Minsk have also begun discussing a major deal to buy Belarusian potash, as Trump announced last week. Coale says Russia is involved in the talks because European sanctions mean Belarusian potash will have to be exported through Russia.
Coale’s plan for Moscow is still in its early stages and aims to break the deadlock in talks between Russia and the United States, Shuster says. In Shuster’s view, it would give Vladimir Putin an easy way to show goodwill and signs of diplomatic progress with the United States without stopping Russia’s strikes on Ukraine. In exchange for the release of prisoners, Washington could offer the Kremlin sanctions relief and a return to trade deals.
Coale believes such deals would help bring about peace: “Economic ties usually result in normality.” Ukraine does not share his optimism. President Volodymyr Zelensky told Shuster he would do his best to “block” any attempt to lift sanctions on Russia before the war ends.
Belarusian opposition leader Svetlana Tikhanovskaya believes lifting sanctions in exchange for prisoners could only encourage authorities in Russia and Belarus to take more hostages:
They can always arrest more people, while the West loses its leverage over these regimes by lifting sanctions and making deals.
Dmitry Muratov, a former Novaya Gazeta editor-in-chief and Nobel Peace Prize laureate, suggested that Coale try his Belarus approach with the Kremlin. Muratov asked Shuster to introduce him to the presidential envoy.
Coale already has a list of Americans held in Russian prisons whose cases Washington could raise in future negotiations. He and Muratov compiled a separate list of Russian political prisoners, journalists, and others convicted for opposing the war. No specific names or possible U.S. concessions have been disclosed.
