articles.title: Ukraine pushes for 'bold action' on Russian assets to plug $78bn shortfall in 2027
articles.body:
Russia's relentless airstrikes are deepening Ukraine's financial gap. As costs rise and the deficit swells, the country is pleading with European allies to tap into the immobilised Russian assets.
Ukraine has urged the European Union to tap into the immobilised Russian assets to help plug the country's financial and military shortfall next year, which could hit a staggering $78 billion (€68.77 billion) if allies fail to step up their contributions.
Sergii Marchenko, Ukraine's finance minister, made the push on Tuesday as he met with representatives from international donors and financial institutions in Brussels.
During the gathering, Marchenko argued that using the pool of Russian assets would be both a practical and fair solution to meet Ukraine's extraordinary wartime costs, protect its debt sustainability and ensure accountability for Moscow's aggression, according to officials with knowledge of the private discussions.
The EU holds €210 billion of these assets, most of it in Euroclear, a depository in Brussels.
The minister recognised the topic was politically difficult and encouraged the bloc to consider a centralised, legally sound framework.
Marchenko delivered a similar message on Monday at a panel hosted by the European Policy Centre (EPC) that examined the idea of transferring the assets from Euroclear into an EU-owned custodian to mitigate risks for Belgium.
"We need our friends, our European politicians, to be brave enough and to make some bold actions," the minister said in his remarks.
"Unfortunately, the war is longer, the war is harder, and we need to provide some resolution of frozen Russian assets or provide other means for us to survive."
Marchenko provided an overview of the dire financial situation that Ukraine faces in 2027.
From the $52.6 billion in financial aid needed from donors, only $20 billion has been covered so far, leaving a $32.6 billion gap. Meanwhile, there is roughly $45 billion in defence expenditure for which allies have not provided guarantees.
Altogether, this creates a $78 billion hole.
The budget crunch, Marchenko explained, is further aggravated by Russia's non-stop attacks, which have severely disrupted ordinary activity, crippled power grids, destroyed factories and impeded tax collection. Moscow has recently begun to target Ukraine's data centres to impair its digital economy and communications system.
At the same time, the blockade in the Black Sea has left Ukrainian farmers without the sea routes they need to sell their grain to clients worldwide. Losses mount with each day maritime trade remains closed off.
"It's the first time since 2022 we realised that we have underperformance in our tax and customs administrations," the minister said.
Loan under pressure
This is not the first time that the assets of the Russian Central Bank, immobilised since February 2022, have come under scrutiny.
Last year, the European Commission tried to channel the assets into a zero-interest credit line for Ukraine. The inventive proposal fell apart in December at a dramatic summit, where Belgium, the chief opponent, mobilised a majority against it.
As a Plan B, EU leaders agreed to set up a €90 billion support loan based on joint debt. The loan has been evenly halved: €45 billion for 2026 and €45 billion for 2027.
But Russia's escalation has rapidly added to the bill.
"We're very happy with the €90 billion," Marchenko said. "But it's not sufficient."
Sweden, the Netherlands, Spain and Poland, backed by the Baltics, have also warned the loan would not be enough and called for "new options" to tap the Russian assets.
Belgium immediately pushed back against the move. Italy and France, two key votes, remain sceptical about touching the sovereign funds, according to diplomats.
The Commission is keen to avoid another defeat and insists the "primary focus" is the disbursement of the €90 billion loan, which has been hampered by the slow pace of reforms in the Ukrainian parliament.
EU officials are frustrated that Ukraine is asking for fresh money when it is not doing the necessary work to unlock the assistance already agreed.
Marta Kos, the European Commissioner for Enlargement, drove the point home during Tuesday's donors' conference.
"Our message to our Ukrainian friends is clear: deliver the agreed reforms, so we can continue supporting you financially," she said in her opening remarks.
"The government, the Rada and institutions across Ukraine need to unite around this collective effort and act with determination to deliver the reforms."
For the past month, the Commission has engaged in intense talks with Ukraine and the International Monetary Fund to pin down the exact scope of the financial shortfall.
The country initially flagged a $27 billion gap in its Ministry of Defence for this year, but this figure has since been downgraded. Marchenko focused his intervention on the needs for 2027, rather than 2026.
The Commission is yet to validate the numbers shared by Kyiv.

articles.title: How the War is Changing the Geography of Iran’s Influence
articles.body:
On Sept. 10, Israel destroyed Hezbollah’s underground command center and weapons stores beneath the Ali al-Tahir ridge in southern Lebanon, about 10 miles from the Lebanon-Israel border. The loss deprived Hezbollah of a fortified position and dealt another blow to Iran’s most important regional ally, which has lost senior commanders and much of its arsenal over the past two years.
Farther south, another part of Iran’s regional network was gaining ground. In Yemen, the Houthis seized territory along the Red Sea coast, bringing them closer to controlling the approaches to Bab al-Mandab, the passage connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
The fall of Bashar al-Assad in Syria in 2024 and Hezbollah’s weakening have diminished Tehran’s influence in the Levant. Yet the wider war has created opportunities for Iran and its partners, particularly around the waterways indispensable for trade and energy exports. Thus, Tehran is losing influence in one arena while acquiring new sources of leverage in another.
Iran’s efforts to control passage through the Strait of Hormuz are only one part of the picture. The Houthis’ expanding reach in the Red Sea gives Tehran’s partners leverage over a strategic waterway, while Iran-aligned armed groups in Iraq can threaten oil pipelines built to bypass these maritime chokepoints.
For Iran’s neighbors, even the routes meant to provide an escape from one danger are exposed to another. Tehran remains under enormous military and economic pressure, but its setbacks in its traditional centers of influence have not ended its ability to impose costs elsewhere.
From the Mediterranean to the Red Sea
In 2014, Yahya Rahim Safavi, a senior adviser to Iran’s then Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, was at a conference of Iran-Iraq War veterans that was broadcast live on state television. He spoke of Iran’s growing reach through Syria and Lebanon. Iran’s “strategic depth” had stretched to the Mediterranean coast and just to the north of Israel, he declared. Hezbollah’s arsenal and the supply corridor through Syria were central to Iran’s “forward defense,” a strategy intended to deter adversaries and keep conflicts away from Iranian territory.
The foundations of that strategy have since been severely weakened. Assad’s removal cost Tehran one of its few state allies and disrupted its ability to resupply Hezbollah, while Israeli operations diminished the group’s capacity to retaliate on Iran’s behalf. Subsequent attacks on Iran itself by Israel and the United States demonstrated the consequences: its regional partners could no longer be counted on to prevent a direct war.
But Iran has been adapting. Even while fighting its own direct war with the U.S., Tehran has worked to develop other sources of regional leverage. On Jun. 8, Esmail Ghaani, commander of the Quds Force, the overseas operations arm of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced a “new security belt” extending from the Strait of Hormuz to Bab al-Mandab and from “the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea.” His statement pointed to a growing emphasis on the ability of Iran and its partners to threaten maritime transit across both waterways.
The Houthis’ capture of Mokha, a port city on the Red Sea coast, and Perim Island, which lies within Bab al-Mandab, gives them a stronger foothold at the southern entrance to the Red Sea. These positions could allow them to monitor passing vessels more closely and deploy weapons near the shipping lanes.
They do not need to halt all traffic to exert influence over the passage. Although the Houthis claim they are targeting only Saudi-linked vessels, the threat of attack alone has driven up insurance costs and forced shipping companies to choose longer routes.
The Houthis have their own agenda and should not be treated as an Iranian proxy acting on Tehran’s instructions. Their domestic motivations remain important: their campaign against rival Yemeni factions aims to consolidate their dominance and attacks on Saudi Arabia seek to force Riyadh to reduce its involvement in Yemen, lift what the Houthis consider a “siege,” and recognize them as the country’s ruling power.
Still, the ties between the Houthis and Tehran have deepened since Oct. 2023, and Iranian support has been central to the development of Houthi military capabilities. Some reports suggest Tehran has sent IRGC commanders, military advisers, and missile and drone equipment to Yemen to strengthen the Houthis’ ability to threaten Red Sea shipping.
Overall, the Houthis increasingly see the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran as a threat to the wider “Axis of Resistance” to which they belong; this translates into a close strategic relationship, even though Tehran may not direct every Houthi operation. As the Houthis see it, supporting Tehran serves both Iran’s and their own interests.
These interests are reinforcing one another. Iran’s disruption of Hormuz has increased the strategic importance of Red Sea export routes, giving the Houthis greater leverage over Saudi Arabia and forcing the kingdom to shift exports back to Hormuz, where—despite a recent significant uptick in traffic—passage remains uncertain. From Iran’s perspective, the goal of pressuring Saudi oil exports is to raise the costs of war for Washington and the global economy, giving President Donald Trump another reason to think twice before escalating the campaign.
Between Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb
For Saudi Arabia, the interaction between Hormuz and Bab-al-Mandab fronts creates a vulnerability. While it is true that “shuttle runs” through the strait have helped Gulf oil exporters get their goods out and eased market pressure, shipments remain at risk of Iranian disruption.
As with the Houthis and Bab al-Mandab, Tehran need not close the strait entirely: intermittent attacks can sustain uncertainty and raise shipping costs. Given Houthi advances in Yemen, diverting exports to Red Sea ports is not necessarily a safer option. Riyadh can shift between routes but cannot entirely evade the risk of disruption.
The vulnerability extends inland. A recent drone attack launched from Iraq damaged three pumping stations on Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline and forced a shutdown. Although the pipeline has resumed partial operations, the message was clear: attacks on this alternative route cannot be ruled out.
Among some Iranian strategists, the attack was also interpreted as a broader warning against building pipeline routes to carry Iraqi oil toward Europe through Turkey and Syria: diverting oil away from the straits would not necessarily put it beyond the reach of Iran and its partners.
The attack was widely attributed to an Iran-backed militia, even though the Islamic Resistance in Iraq—an umbrella grouping of Iran-aligned factions—denied involvement. Since the war began in February, the IRGC reportedly has mobilized smaller cells of Iraqi Shiite fighters operating under its command, giving Tehran a more direct role in operations from Iraqi territory.
There may well not be a unified chain of command across the Iranian, Yemeni, and Iraqi fronts, yet attacks from Iraqi territory must be seen as part of a broader campaign, adding to both Houthi pressure in the Red Sea and Iranian disruption in Hormuz. The cost to Baghdad is high, as it is unable to prevent armed factions from launching attacks that expose Iraq to retaliation and undermine its relations with Gulf neighbors. The resulting tensions could also serve Tehran’s interest in limiting its Gulf rivals’ influence in Iraq.
Together, these developments help explain Tehran’s defiant posture, as it feels it can threaten Saudi exports in numerous ways and thereby heighten the economic costs of the war for the United States and its partners.
This has strengthened the argument within the Iranian leadership that they should hold firm and, with time, improve their bargaining position in potential negotiations with Washington. The problem with this argument is that mounting costs for its adversaries do not necessarily mean Iran can afford a prolonged confrontation.
The costs of waiting
Trump’s campaign has so far failed to force Iran to accept American terms, while giving Tehran and its partners new opportunities to threaten the global economy. The longer the confrontation continues, the greater the likelihood that Tehran will respond by deepening military coordination with its non-state partners and escalating attacks, directly or through them. In this sense, Washington should have an interest in reaching a settlement before such cooperation becomes more entrenched and the confrontation spreads further.
But Tehran risks drawing the wrong conclusion from this dynamic. Recent developments may encourage Iranian leaders to demand more and offer less, believing that mounting economic costs will eventually force Trump to retreat. But such a scenario is far from being inevitable. Washington might instead respond with further attacks or tighter enforcement of the blockade. Each side would then treat the other’s refusal to concede as reason to intensify pressure, prolonging an uneasy standoff while making an agreement even more difficult.
Iran would be wrong to assume that time will improve its position. Its economy continues to bear the costs of the blockade, and disrupting its neighbors’ exports does nothing to finance its own recovery. Saudi Arabia will resist any arrangement that leaves its access to global markets dependent on Iranian and Houthi restraint. If Riyadh concludes that a negotiated deal would formalize that dependence, it could shift toward more open support for American military and economic pressure on Iran.
Saudi resistance to a planned Oman meeting among Iranian and Gulf officials earlier this month already points to limitations in Iran’s strategy. An emerging Iran-Oman agreement over the Strait of Hormuz ostensibly offered a basis for negotiations over maritime passage, but Gulf governments—and notably Riyadh—resisted arrangements that, in their eyes, would legitimize Iran’s unacceptable claim to control transit in the waterway.
Although their vulnerability gave them an urgent reason to seek an agreement, it also led them to resist a deal on terms that would entrench Iran’s dominance. Their refusal to attend showed that Iran’s ability to disrupt their trade has not translated into acceptance of Iranian terms.
Iran’s expanding regional reach, both directly and through its partners, strengthens its position in negotiations. But it also makes it all the more necessary to reassure its neighbors. A settlement will remain difficult as long as Tehran expects those neighbors to accept lasting uncertainty over their legitimate maritime rights in exchange for relief from the immediate threat of disruption.

articles.title: Between two chokepoints: Egypt's growing Red Sea dilemma
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Between two chokepoints: Egypt's growing Red Sea dilemma
Seven months into the US-Israel war on Iran, Egypt finds itself increasingly exposed to the pressures of a wider regional conflagration.
The Houthis’ recent offensive to consolidate control over Bab al-Mandeb poses serious risks for Cairo, which has already experienced the economic fallout of Houthi attacks on maritime traffic.
In late 2023, when the Houthis targeted commercial shipping in response to Israel’s war on Gaza, the campaign sharply curtailed traffic through the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.
According to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the turmoil reduced Egypt’s Suez Canal revenues by over $6 billion in 2024.
Traffic through the canal has since recovered, with transits exceeding 1,200 in both July and August. August also marked the busiest month since December 2023.
Prolonged disruption could, however, once again constrain one of Egypt’s key sources of foreign currency. A deterioration in Red Sea security would also carry wider economic, political, and security consequences for the broader region.
Houthis seek to maximise Red Sea gains
The Houthis’ expanding offensive along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including their capture of strategically important territory around Mocha and the islands of Mayun (Perim) and Hanish, is aimed at cementing their position around Bab al-Mandeb.
“They know that holding the coast for long may be difficult, which is why they are trying to entrench themselves by securing the highlands overlooking Bab al-Mandeb and cutting the strategic lines connecting Aden and Taiz, which would obstruct the ability to send reinforcements to Mokha,” Yasmeen El Eryani, Executive Director for Knowledge Production at the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies, told The New Arab.
This strategy also reinforces a broader trend in contemporary conflict: the weaponisation of economic interdependence. Recent months have demonstrated the extent of the global economy’s dependence on a limited number of strategic infrastructure networks and maritime chokepoints.
This asymmetry has created opportunities for conventionally weaker actors to generate outsized political gains. Iran’s use of the Strait of Hormuz underscored the strategic leverage that can be derived from weaponising maritime chokepoints.
That logic is particularly relevant to the Red Sea, where the Houthis are closely watching developments around the Strait of Hormuz with a growing awareness that they do not need uncontested control of the entire maritime corridor to impose real costs on global shipping and energy markets. The ability to generate sufficient uncertainty can itself become a major strategic tool.
“The Houthis don’t yet want to strangle all shipping, rather, they seek to leave open the possibility that things could go in that direction if certain demands aren’t met. For now, it serves them better if the threat remains veiled,” Alia Brahimi, Non-resident Senior Fellow at the Atlantic Council, told The New Arab.
Prospects of prolonged disruption weigh heavily on Cairo’s strategic calculations. Consistent with its cautious posture since the US-Israel war on Iran began, Egypt has approached the latest escalation with strategic restraint.
In response to the latest round of Houthi attacks, Cairo established a specialised crisis cell to monitor developments and doubled down on regional diplomacy. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s visit to Cairo in mid-September reflected continued close bilateral coordination.
Multilaterally, the regional quartet (R4), comprising Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan, remains active, convening for the sixth time on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty also met with his Omani counterpart, stressing Egypt’s solidarity with Saudi Arabia and affirming Cairo’s commitment to supporting regional de-escalation.
“Egypt has much to lose from further escalation of regional hostilities, particularly in the Red Sea. This suggests Cairo will likely continue pursuing an intermediary role alongside other regional actors with similar interests, including Oman, Pakistan, Turkey, and Qatar,” Giorgio Cafiero, CEO of Gulf State Analytics, told The New Arab.
The Houthis’ growing confidence, however, cannot be separated from Iran’s broader regional strategy. With Hamas and Hezbollah’s capabilities severely degraded, the Houthis have become a vital lever for Tehran to exert pressure and project power across the region.
Interconnected regional conflict theatres
The Houthis’ increasingly assertive approach to Bab al-Mandeb comes at a strategically significant moment, ahead of the US midterm elections.
With peace negotiations stalled and fears of renewed hostilities mounting, “the Houthis gave themselves a tight timeline to conduct the Bab al-Mandeb operation because, for it to yield optimal results for the Houthis and Iran, it needed to happen ahead of the US midterms, so that it could be used as leverage in Iran-US negotiations,” El Eryani told The New Arab.
These developments illustrate how multiple theatres can be exploited simultaneously, through allied groups, with far-reaching economic and security repercussions.
Previously relatively shielded from the direct effects of the Iran war, Egypt now faces growing challenges from escalating tensions in the Red Sea. Cairo has thus far avoided isolating or antagonising any regional players.
This caution is reinforced by the legacy of Egypt’s 1960s intervention in Yemen, which cost the lives of more than 10,000 Egyptian soldiers and shaped a longstanding preference for diplomatic engagement and close coordination with regional partners over direct military intervention.
Egypt is likely to remain aligned with regional partners, providing political and potentially targeted military support, as it did through naval participation in the 2015 Operation Decisive Storm and through its membership in the Saudi-led Multinational Maritime Defence Alliance, established earlier this year to strengthen maritime security and protect international shipping and energy routes in the Red Sea, Bab al-Mandeb, and Gulf of Aden.
“But the pressure to act is being applied from many directions, and the real risk is that Egypt accidentally becomes entrapped by the escalatory logic of the conflict more generally,” said Brahimi.
The limits of regional alliances
The Houthis’ attacks on Saudi Arabia marked the first real test of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, struck last month between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan. The test revealed the enduring challenges of activating joint regional defence frameworks.
While signatories mobilised rhetorically in response to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, whether that translates into a coordinated joint response remains to be seen.
Egypt remains outside the framework, but this challenging landscape will likely further complicate Cairo’s prospective role in joint defence frameworks, particularly Article 5-style agreements that create commitments to direct intervention.
Any decision to intervene would require caution. Cairo is navigating the Red Sea on two simultaneous fronts, as an economic lifeline and a strategic theatre in which competing regional interests intersect. This creates significant constraints on the scope of direct Egyptian involvement.
These dynamics leave Egypt with a narrow set of options. Further escalation in the Red Sea would expose the Egyptian economy to direct economic and security risks, but the costs of direct intervention remain high.
Cairo is therefore likely to continue relying on its diplomatic channels, intelligence-sharing networks, and naval capabilities while closely monitoring developments.
Ultimately, Egypt’s strategy will be shaped by how far the Houthis and the wider Iran war expand, and how directly the conflict spills over into Egypt’s strategic interests.
Hana Elshehaby is a Senior Research Assistant for the Middle East Council on Global Affairs. She is also a Non-Resident Fellow at the Institute for Middle East Options

articles.title: What to Know About the Pentagon Breach Affecting Millions
articles.body:
A reported monthslong breach in the Defense Department’s human resources database exposed personal information of millions of military personnel and those related to them, including their Social Security numbers and job details.
A Pentagon official confirmed to TIME Tuesday that some 2.76 million “living individuals” and 294,000 “deceased individuals” have been affected by the breach at the Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC).
The breach was first reported by defense-focused news publication Military Times on Thursday, citing a breach notification letter to a person whose information was in the affected files.
It remains unclear what particular files were accessed and who was behind the incident. The Defense Department official told TIME that individuals whose personal information were accessed had been notified by mail.
The length of the breach and the amount of personal information exposed present a security risk for many personnel linked with the department, and some experts say it makes other security compromises, like phishing attempts, easier for bad actors.
What we know about the breach
The DMDC collates personnel, manpower, training, financial, and other data for the Defense Department for healthcare, retirement funding, and other administrative needs. Its website says that based on FY2024 data, it has the records of more than 60 million people—including the military, civilians, contractors, family members, retirees, and veterans.
But the Military Times reviewed a Sept. 18 letter from the DMDC notifying its recipient of a data breach. The letter reportedly said it discovered on July 16 a security vulnerability in the center’s file-sharing system.
The notice reportedly details that between October 2025 and the time of discovery, some “unauthorized users” accessed files on a server containing the personal information. The type of personal information varies from names to dates of birth, contact information, and others.
DMDC then said it updated the file-sharing system to address the vulnerability. The letter reportedly added that there has been no indication of misuse of the recipient’s information.
Not the first hack
The latest incident involving Pentagon data emerged as the FBI confirmed it was looking into criminal hacking group ShinyHunters’s apparent attack on its jobs website. The group claimed to have stolen “very sensitive data” on nearly all agents and job applicants in response to an FBI notice about them issued in May. (ShinyHunters were also behind a high-profile hack in May of education platform Canvas.)
It’s still unclear how massive the previous FBI breach was, but a New York Times analysis found that it may have involved the stealing of home addresses, Social Security numbers, and job assignments, on top of other personally identifiable information. Reuters reported last week that the hackers claimed they have obtained about 2-3 terabytes of data. Some of the data Reuters reviewed also revealed details of assignments to specific field offices, as well as FBI units engaged in high-stakes intelligence, security, or counterespionage work, which risks endangering national security.
In a statement to 404 Media and the Times, the FBI said it was “working around the clock to investigate the cyber incident involving FBIJobs.gov and is in regular communication with anyone who may be impacted—including multiple bureau-wide communications within 24 hours of public reporting.”
The FBI incident also follows a breach that may have exposed more than 153 million driver’s licenses in the U.S. and Canada.
What affected personnel can do
Security experts have previously warned that access to troves of records poses a massive security risk, especially if these fall into the hands of foreign actors.
Justin Sherman, a senior associate at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote about the license data breach earlier this month: “It can be tempting to dismiss the next hack of a database as ‘just another data breach.’... But breaches do not exist in a vacuum.”
The DMDC said in its notice to affected personnel that it was offering year-long credit monitoring and identity-restoration services through IDX, a private firm contracted by the department. The defense official said in a statement to TIME that individuals with questions should contact IDX at https://response.idx.us/DMDC or 1-855-744-4556.
According to the Federal Trade Commission, anyone could place a free credit freeze with each of the three major credit bureaus—Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion.
Active duty personnel and National Guard members could also get free electronic credit monitoring to spot problems that could stem from identity theft.

Supreme court allows Trump to resume deporting people to third countries for now while justices weigh policy
The supreme court has allowed the Trump administration to resume deporting people to countries other than their own without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face, bolstering a tool Donald Trump has used for rapid expulsions as part of his immigration crackdown.
The justices granted the DOJ’s request to halt Boston-based US district judge Brian Murphy’s ruling that the Department of Homeland Security’s policy to remove migrants to so-called third countries is unlawful, while the administration appeals the matter to the supreme court. They also agreed to hear arguments in the dispute in December, with a formal ruling on policy to follow.
Its three liberal justices dissented from the decision.
Federal attorneys said the lower-court decision forced the cancellation of a deportation flight carrying about 70 people bound for three countries.
The justices previously allowed the deportation flights, a core Trump administration policy, to temporarily continue when the case came before them last year. In another win for the administration, the supreme court subsequently lifted limits the judge had imposed to protect a group of men from being sent to South Sudan.
More than 25,000 people have been deported to 29 countries under the policy implemented last year, according to a tally by human rights groups, with the vast majority going to Mexico.
The administration has also carried out third-country deportations to politically unstable South Sudan, which the US state department urges Americans to avoid due to the risks of crime, kidnapping and armed conflict, as well as Uganda, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia, the Central African Republic, and other nations.
Reacting to the decision, attorney general Todd Blanche has just said on X:
Now for the second time, SCOTUS just granted our stay in conducting all third-country removals of illegal aliens. Again, this is entirely lawful and a critical tool for immigration enforcement. Unlike the lower court, SCOTUS waited to hear from both sides before making the decision.
To be clear, the supreme court majority has decided to allow the deportations to resume pending the final outcome of the litigation, i.e. while it hears arguments and then decides whether or not the policy is lawful.
Democrat Chris Van Hollen, of Maryland, and 24 other senators have introduced a resolution demanding that the US government do a human rights assessment of the conduct of the government of Israel in the occupied West Bank, after the “absolutely outrageous” killings of nine American citizens in the last four years, “either by violent Israeli settlers or Israeli security forces”.
“We’ve seen no accountability, no justice,” Van Hollen says in a video shared on social media, where he also calls for the immediate release of the American citizens wrongfully detained there.
Accusing the Israeli government of “gross violations of human rights”, he highlights its treatment of Palestinian people:
Imagine, if we can’t get the Israeli government to ensure accountability and justice when American citizens are killed, imagine the situation for Palestinians, who do not hold an American passport. Who are killed with impunity, whose houses and cars are burned, whose places of worship are burned, and you have the government of Israel trying to push them all off their lands in what is clearly a policy of ethnic cleansing.
Supreme court allows Trump to resume deporting people to third countries for now while justices weigh policy
The supreme court has allowed the Trump administration to resume deporting people to countries other than their own without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face, bolstering a tool Donald Trump has used for rapid expulsions as part of his immigration crackdown.
The justices granted the DOJ’s request to halt Boston-based US district judge Brian Murphy’s ruling that the Department of Homeland Security’s policy to remove migrants to so-called third countries is unlawful, while the administration appeals the matter to the supreme court. They also agreed to hear arguments in the dispute in December, with a formal ruling on policy to follow.
Its three liberal justices dissented from the decision.
Federal attorneys said the lower-court decision forced the cancellation of a deportation flight carrying about 70 people bound for three countries.
The justices previously allowed the deportation flights, a core Trump administration policy, to temporarily continue when the case came before them last year. In another win for the administration, the supreme court subsequently lifted limits the judge had imposed to protect a group of men from being sent to South Sudan.
More than 25,000 people have been deported to 29 countries under the policy implemented last year, according to a tally by human rights groups, with the vast majority going to Mexico.
The administration has also carried out third-country deportations to politically unstable South Sudan, which the US state department urges Americans to avoid due to the risks of crime, kidnapping and armed conflict, as well as Uganda, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia, the Central African Republic, and other nations.
Robert F Kennedy Jr laid out an expansive vision for collecting, sharing and analyzing US health information at a Maha event hosted by a close ally and outspoken anti-vaccine activist.
Medical and lifestyle data, from doctor’s visits to exercise, should be connected and shared with the government and independent researchers, where it can be searched by AI – including potential links between vaccines and health outcomes including autism and mortality, suggested Kennedy, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine skeptic.
“We need to use America’s health data to determine whether the food we eat, the chemicals we encounter, the vaccines that we’re administering, the other environmental and lifestyle exposures are contributing in one way or another to the chronic disease epidemic,” Kennedy said at an event with the Maha Institute on Monday, with about two dozen people tuning into the live stream.
The Maha Institute is headed by Mark Gorton, who called himself “the boldest anti-vaxxer in the anti-vax conference” two weeks ago. The institute was co-founded by Tony Lyons, whose publishing house gave $4m to Kennedy through various Maha foundations with funding from political contributions and health-related corporations, according to reporting by the New York Times.
Kennedy has focused on pulling together data from all of the agencies he oversees, including the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS).
Trump speaks after meeting with AI company executives
Speaking after a meeting with several AI company executives, Donald Trump said that there “was a lot of commonality in this room”.
A reminder that some of those at today’s meeting include Open AI’s Sam Altman, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, Elon Musk, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang.
When it comes to further guardrails on development, the president said that “tremendous self-regulation” should be the path forward, compared with the calls that there should be greater congressional oversight.
On the topic of datacenters, Trump insisted that the structures – which are used to house thousands of energy-intensive servers for tech companies – “are going to be very popular”.
This, despite frequent polling which shows that an overwhelming majority of Americans do not approve of more datacenter construction in their communities.
“The areas with datacenters have become very rich,” Trump claimed, without citing any evidence. “People have become very rich. Their taxes have gone down, not up, and a lot of good things have happened.”
In fact, several areas that are the site of datacenter development have raised concerns about water quality, noise pollution and potential impact on their electricity bills.
Jack Smith faced Senate lawmakers on the judiciary committee for a contentious hearing that saw a number of Republicans accuse the former special prosecutor of perjury, and conducting a political witch-hunt against Donald Trump when he secured two indictments against the president that were later dismissed when he took office. Many GOP lawmakers hurled insults and accusations, with little evidence, at Smith. The former special counsel stood by his findings, and said that his investigations found “proof beyond a reasonable doubt” that Trump engaged in criminal activity. He also fended off allegations about the legality of procuring call toll records – and explained several times what these are and aren’t – outlined the persistent attacks he and former colleagues have faced from lawmakers and the president in the years since he prosecuted Trump and defended himself against the accusations that his work was politically motivated. Democrats, meanwhile, blasted their colleagues for peddling “the Big Lie” and called the hearing a “farce”.
In Washington, Trump said the US ‘can’t stifle’ AI as he unveiled a new tool to streamline federal government information. The president made his views on any guardrails on AI development clear again, after previously branding the calls as a “hoax”. Also today, Trump met with several AI company CEOs at the White House, alongside Republican House speaker Mike Johnson.
Trump also used the opportunity – now a little more than a month away from the midterm elections – to repeat his claim that the war with Iran will be over “very soon”. This despite another week of stalled negotiations between Washington and Tehran via mediators. “They’re failing very badly,” the president said. “They will not have a nuclear weapon. And oil prices are going to be tumbling down, just like they were before.” He again referred to the conflict as a “little excursion”. A reminder the war is now in its seventh month, and has caused a global energy crisis that has seen the average price of a gallon of gas increase by a dollar.
A Republican senator blocked a bipartisan bill that would have prevented Donald Trump from demolishing the Kennedy Center without the approval of Congress. Mike Lee, of Utah, objected when the Oregon Democrat Jeff Merkley asked the Senate to pass the Protecting Presidential Memorials Act by unanimous consent. The bill, co-written with the Alaska Republican Lisa Murkowski, would have banned the demolition of any presidential memorial designated by Congress, including the Lincoln and Jefferson memorials, unless lawmakers explicitly approved it.
Smith pushed back against a number of Josh Hawley’s accusations, including the process the former special prosecutor went about to get records from the National Archives, which included text messages between White House officials and 44 members of Congress
“That was a request for White House phones,” Smith said, noting that these happened to have contacts with members of Congress in it. “It was also inaccurate to state that our indictment happened on 2 October. We indicted that case in August [2023],” Smith said, noting that he and his team and consulted with the Public Integrity Section of the justice department, who “ultimately concurred” that they had “followed the election year sensitivities policy”.
Hawley accuses Smith of attempting to 'interfere' with presidential election through Trump investigations
Josh Hawley – a Republican senator and fierce Trump ally – launched into his critiques of Smith from the jump.
“Your investigation, so-called, your prosecution, so-called, was nothing other than an attempt to interfere politically in a presidential election in the United States of America,” Hawley said, repeating many right-wing conspiracies about Smith’s motivations. “You twice indicted a presidential candidate.”
When Thom Tillis, the outgoing Republican senator from North Carolina, asked Smith about whether there was anything he would have changed in the way he handled his investigations into Donald Trump, the former special prosecutor said that he learned, throughout his inquiries, that if he only stuck to confining his comments to the courtoom “people can unfairly malign your team and unfairly malign you and your case”.
He added:
There are things being put out daily that are patently untrue … I’m not advocating that prosecutors in the future start going on the internet every day responding to comments … I do agree that prosecutors in the future need to learn to be able to communicate to the outside world because I believe strongly we did our investigation the right way, but I limited myself in who I talked to about that.
Jack Smith tells Darline Graham her brother would have 'likely' been a witness in the case against Trump
Ariana Baio
Republican senator Darline Graham, the sister of late senator Lindsey Graham, used her time questioning Jack Smith to accuse the former special counsel of adding “stress” to her brother’s life through subpoenas.
The South Carolina senator, appointed to replace her brother who died in July, told Smith that he should be “ashamed” of himself and that it made her “sick” to think that Smith’s subpoenas of Lindsey Graham’s phone records would have stressed him out.
“Do you really believe that Lindsey was going to destroy evidence that was not even in his possession?” Darline Graham asked.
But Smith responded, saying Lindsey Graham was “a patriot” and was not the target of his investigation.
“He likely would have been a witness in our case,” Smith added.
Cory Booker rails against Republicans 'gaslighting' public by perpetuating lie that Trump won 2020 election
Back at the hearing, Democratic senator Cory Booker accused Republicans of “a farce”, levelling that they were “gaslighting” the public by “continuing to perpetuate the big lie in America that Donald Trump was somehow cheated out of the 2020 election.”
This big lie has gone on [long] enough. We have people who are serving at the highest offices in the land that repeat the big lie. We have people running for office in the Republican party that can’t even tell the truth.
And today’s farce – today’s gaslighting – cannot obscure the mountain of evidence and what Americans saw with their own eyes.
A visibly frustrated Booker lamented that this was unfair to Jack Smith and his family, but also to the American people who continue to struggle with problems including high gas prices, lack of health insurance coverage, and childcare costs.
The New Jersey senator ended, addressing Smith:
What do the Republicans in control of Congress do with their closing statement before an election? They carry out the big lie. They persecute prosecutors. They do Trump’s bidding. They choose Trump over truth, corruption and crimes over the constitution, and I’ve had enough of it.
This hearing is a farce. And I’m sorry for what you and your family are enduring as a result.
Utah Republican blocks bill to ban Trump from demolishing Kennedy Center without Congress’s approval
Joseph Gedeon
Away from the hearing for a moment, a Republican senator last night blocked a bipartisan bill that would have prevented Donald Trump from demolishing the Kennedy Center without the approval of Congress.
Mike Lee, of Utah, objected when the Oregon Democrat Jeff Merkley asked the Senate to pass the Protecting Presidential Memorials Act by unanimous consent. The bill, co-written with the Alaska Republican Lisa Murkowski, would have banned the demolition of any presidential memorial designated by Congress, including the Lincoln and Jefferson memorials, unless lawmakers explicitly approved it.
“First, he destroyed its programming, and now, he wants to destroy the building itself,” Merkley wrote in a statement. “All because the law says Trump can’t put his name on the building.” He called the president’s threats “straight out of the authoritarian playbook”.
Murkowski, who chairs the appropriations subcommittee that funds the center, said last week that lawmakers had authorized and funded substantial renovation work, but “what was not authorized is a demolition of the Kennedy Center”.
Here’s Joseph’s report on the latest twist in one of the longest running legal sagas of Trump’s second term:
Ted Cruz angrily questions Jack Smith, says Javert from Les Mis would look in 'astonishment'
Ariana Baio
Republican senator Ted Cruz used his time to admonish Jack Smith for weaponizing the justice department to subpoena Republican members of Congress and conservative organizations during his investigation into Trump.
Cruz insinuated that Smith had used his power as the special counsel to target Republicans, asking Smith, “Is it a crime to be a Republican?” Smith replied: “Absolutely not.”
Cruz became increasingly angry with Smith during questioning, speaking over Smith as he tried to answer questions.
“Javert from Les Mis would look at you with astonishment,” Cruz told Smith.
Throughout Smith’s hearing, Republican senators have repeatedly brought up Timothy Thibault, a former FBI agent who was in charge of the Arctic Frost investigation and accused of political bias.
Republican senator Katie Britt asked Smith multiple times to confirm or deny whether Thibault had engaged in political bias, even though Thibault retired from the FBI months before Smith was made special counsel.
Thibault oversaw paperwork to open the election conspiracy case known as Arctic Frost, which has become an increasingly polarizing topic among lawmakers. Thibault was accused of making political statements on social media, which some Republicans have used to point to a larger accusation that the Biden administration weaponized the Justice Department.
Thibault denied accusations that political partisanship impacted his work.
Senator Chris Coons, a Democrat, asked Smith about his work with Republicans throughout his investigation into Donald Trump’s attempts to overturn the 2020 election.
The former special prosecutor said he found it “very hard” to understand why his probe was considered to be partisan when the “strongest witnesses” were Republicans like Rusty Bowers, a former Arizona state representative, and former vice-president Mike Pence.
“The criminal scheme we investigated was predicated upon Donald Trump preying on party loyalty. He preyed on party loyalty and fear,” Smith said. “The reality is, one of the reasons, our democracy held up. One of the reasons he was not able to take power, even though, he was seeking to do these things is because Republicans stood up.”

articles.title: The United States and the United Kingdom sank a decommissioned American frigate off the coast of Scotland — media reports
articles.body:
The United States and the United Kingdom sank a decommissioned American frigate off the coast of Scotland — media reports
Kyiv • UNN
American and British forces attacked the decommissioned USS Klakring with missiles and a torpedo off Scotland. The ship sank at a depth of 1.8 km.
The U.S. and British navies sank the decommissioned American frigate USS Klakring during the joint Atlantic Thunder 2026 exercise near the Hebrides, UNN reports, citing Bild.
Details
The ship was attacked from the sea, air, and underwater: the American destroyer USS Paul Ignatius launched the anti-ship version of the SM-6 missile, the British HMS Portland fired a Naval Strike missile, and a Wildcat helicopter used a Sea Venom missile against a surface target for the first time.
The final strike was delivered by the American nuclear-powered submarine USS Massachusetts with a heavy Mk 48 torpedo. The former warship then sank approximately 150 nautical miles from the northwest coast of Scotland and came to rest on the seabed at a depth of about 1.8 kilometers.
USS Klakring served in the U.S. Navy from 1983 to 2013. Uncrewed underwater vehicles will now survey the wreckage so that experts can assess the impact of different types of weaponry.
Before the sinking, potentially environmentally hazardous materials were removed from the frigate. As the specialist publication Navy Lookout notes, the use of an American ship was explained, among other things, by the division of costs: the United States paid for preparing and transporting the frigate across the Atlantic, while the United Kingdom paid for use of the range.

articles.title: US tells Lebanon Hezbollah disarmament efforts 'not enough'
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US tells Lebanon Hezbollah disarmament efforts 'not enough'
Lebanon has received negative signals from the United States over its efforts to bring Hezbollah's weapons under state control, with Washington warning that Israel intends to continue its military operations in the south, The New Arab has learned.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam received several messages while in New York on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, including warnings from US officials that Israel intends to maintain the security zone it has established in southern Lebanon.
Washington conveyed that Israel would continue its operations "as long as the Lebanese state does not take serious action to disarm Hezbollah", according to information obtained by TNA, and that it remains determined to destroy the group's military infrastructure.
US officials also told Salam that the steps taken by the Lebanese government so far were insufficient and that efforts to bring all weapons under state control must be accelerated.
According to the information obtained by TNA, Washington called for a firmer approach to the issue, warning that the situation could deteriorate further otherwise.
The warnings come as southern Lebanon faces near-daily Israeli escalation, with Israel stepping up its operations and insisting on maintaining the security zone it has established in the south.
Prospects for a solution are meanwhile receding, at least until Israel's parliamentary elections on 27 October.
Salam also received several messages of support, particularly from Arab and European countries, backing the government's decisions and Lebanon's demands for Israel to halt its attacks and withdraw from occupied Lebanese territory.
There was also support for the need to fill any security vacuum in southern Lebanon if the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) expires without renewal, with efforts expected to intensify in the coming period to find a solution to the crisis.
Hezbollah sets conditions for weapons talks
Attention is meanwhile turning to Hezbollah and whether the group could enter into a confrontation with Israel, particularly if Israeli military operations intensify.
Such a scenario remains unlikely in the near term, however, as Hezbollah is currently looking to developments between the US and Iran, with Tehran making Lebanon a key issue in its negotiations.
Hezbollah parliamentary sources told The New Arab that the group was "monitoring all developments, and its eyes will remain on the field. Iran remains committed to the Lebanon issue and will not abandon it, which is what should be relied upon rather than direct negotiations with the enemy".
They added that the Lebanese state should return to indirect negotiations with Israel and correct the course of the talks.
The sources said Hezbollah was open to discussing the issue of its weapons domestically and as part of a national defence strategy.
However, they said a complete halt to Israeli attacks and Israel's withdrawal from all Lebanese territory must come first.
Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem on Sunday renewed his call for Lebanese authorities to end what he described as concessions and review the course of negotiations, calling for direct talks to be suspended in favour of indirect negotiations.
His comments came on the second anniversary of the assassination of former Hezbollah secretary-generals Hassan Nasrallah and Hashem Safieddine.
"Let it be clear, Lebanon without resistance will disappear; the enemy wants all of Lebanon," Qassem said.
"Lebanon can only remain through its liberation and unity and the cooperation of its components. Whoever bets on retaining a part of Lebanon in exchange for abandoning the other part of the land or people is deluded."
Israel steps up attacks on southern Lebanon
Israeli forces carried out a series of attacks on several areas of southern Lebanon in recent hours, including the use of an Apache attack helicopter in a strike for the first time during the latest escalation.
The helicopter struck a commercial centre on the main road between the towns of Shoukine and Mifdoun in the Nabatieh district.
Israeli forces also carried out air strikes on Wadi Zibqin, Talouseh, Mais al-Jabal and the Al-Dabsh area, while artillery fire targeted Wadi Saluki, the outskirts of Kfar Tibnit and Nabatieh al-Fawqa, Al-Mansouri and Wadi Zibqin.
Israeli forces also opened machine-gun fire towards the outskirts of Kfar Shuba in the Azrael area, as well as Sarbin and the Al-Sadana area.
An explosion was also carried out by Israeli forces in Mais al-Jabal, while illumination flares were fired over Hadatha-Haris and Wadi Saluki.
The escalation comes as Israeli media reports suggest southern Lebanon could enter a new phase in the coming days following the completion of what Israel described as "clearing" operations on the Ali al-Taher heights and the destruction of Hezbollah infrastructure in the area.
Direct negotiations remain suspended despite Washington previously announcing that talks would take place in October.

articles.title: Gastein health conference gets underway
articles.body:
Want to receive this newsletter straight to your inbox? Sign up here to receive the reporting and intel from the Gastein Health Forum.
SNEAK PEEK
— Clemens Martin Auer, president of the European Health Forum Gastein, calls for more action ahead of a four-day health conference.
— The health committee wants action on rare diseases and cancer, as watered-down wording over alcohol spurred controversy.
Advertisement
— U.S. tariffs of up to 100% on pharmaceuticals and their ingredients are set to kick in.
Welcome to Tuesday’s Morning Health Care! It’s the first day of Gastein and Claudia and I will be here all week, so we’re going to need gossip to survive. There are rumors about a place where people dance in a cage to let their hair down; if you know anything, do tell. What happens in Gastein …
A LITTLE LESS CONVERSATION, A LITTLE MORE ACTION: The slow implementation and inefficiency of health policy across Europe is hampering the bloc’s ability to respond to major challenges like climate change, health security, AI and workforce issues, says Clemens Martin Auer, the president of the European Health Forum Gastein. Europe doesn’t have a lack of ideas or technical skills to tackle major problems facing the sector, but rather an implementation problem, he told Morning Health Care in an interview ahead of his last conference as head of the forum, with his final day on Oct. 31. “The older I get, the more impatient I am with the slowness of our policy implementations,” he said.
More action needed: As health experts, industry representatives, and everyone in between descend on Gastein, Austria, for a four-day health conference, Auer is calling for more action. “We are living in really challenging times, and my observation is that we don't do enough to change the situation.”
Pharma: Capricious U.S. health policies, including a push by the Trump administration to reduce domestic drug prices (more on this below), were creating global uncertainty and impacting where drugmakers were investing, Auer said, pointing to increasing investment in China. Health systems in Europe could only be counterbalanced if countries were willing to pay more for products like generics to shore up supply chains, he said. “If you want to safeguard that supply, then you have to be willing to pay more for them.” His comments come as the pharma industry is set to play a major role at the conference across multiple panels, with U.S. policies and European drug prices running as an undercurrent in most major discussions on health security, accessibility, and competitiveness.
Advertisement
Competitiveness: Auer pointed to the Draghi report, which proposed a plan to increase competitiveness more than two years ago. “ Do we see any implementation, substantial implementation? The economic numbers and data are getting worse.”
Health security: Auer also expressed frustration at a lack of action to address the threat to health infrastructure. He called for intelligence sharing and greater cooperation between the defense and health sectors, including shoring up pharmaceutical supply chains to reduce reliance on external sources. “The face of war is changing, the means of war are changing,” he said, pointing to hybrid warfare like cyberattacks and drones. “The security people have to share the information with the health sector, and the health sector has to be open to take it on, act accordingly and put up their measures for more security.”
POLITICAL ADVERTISEMENT
Sponsor: European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA)
The political advertisement is linked to the EU Biotech Act
SANT ADOPTS CANCER REPORT: Lawmakers in the public health committee on Monday adopted a report on cancer, calling for dedicated funding in the next multiannual financial framework, action on prevention, and equal access to cancer screening, diagnosis and treatment across the EU.
Rocky negotiations: The report was at the center of controversy over its language on alcohol. “When it comes to cancer, there is no safe level of alcohol consumption,” said the Association of European Cancer Leagues. “By referring to 'levels exceeding scientifically established health recommendations', the report implies there is a safe threshold. That is misleading.”
Rare diseases vote: MEPs want a dedicated law to improve diagnosis of rare diseases, ensure equal access to treatment, and place greater emphasis on patient care, with 33 votes in favor, three against, and five abstentions on a legislative initiative resolution in the health committee. Rare diseases affect tens of millions of people across Europe, with three in four of those living with one being children. The committee’s recommendations and legislative initiative report will be tabled for a vote at the next European Parliament plenary. You can read the full details of the committee’s plan here.
MORE ALCOHOL DRAMA: Civil society groups are calling out a European Parliament event on the role of wine in health policy, which they say is “inappropriate” and poorly timed as it coincides with World Heart Day.
Advertisement
Context: The event, taking place today, is organized by the European Committee of Wine Companies and Socialists & Democrats MEP Dario Nardella. It brings together lawmakers, industry and researchers “to explore how the latest scientific evidence can better inform policymaking and contribute to a more nuanced discussion on the role of wine as part of a healthy lifestyle.”
But to civil societies, it sends the wrong message: “Civil society organisations working to reduce alcohol-related harm in Europe object to events like this, which give commercial interests a seat at the agenda-setting table of EU public health policy,” they wrote in a statement.
Not the time: They also criticize the timing of the event on World Heart Day. “European public health organisations consider it wholly inappropriate that an MEP would give the alcohol industry a platform in a health policy debate, particularly on a day dedicated to raising awareness of cardiovascular disease and its prevention,” they add.
Encouraging an open discussion: “Today's event brings scientists together to discuss evidence on health, diet and longevity, and this kind of debate strengthens prevention,” Nardella told Morning Health Care. “Good public policy needs to be proportionate and evidence-based, and it should distinguish between harmful consumption and moderate consumption within a balanced lifestyle and a traditional food culture like ours. Moderation is the key to the consumption of everything, not just alcohol.” He added that the event falling on World Heart Day was a coincidence.
Coincidence? "On World Heart Day, I would argue this debate is particularly relevant, not inappropriate … an open and transparent dialogue with all relevant stakeholders is an important part of a whole-of-society approach to health," said Ignacio Sánchez Recarte, secretary general of the European Committee of Wine Companies.
Signed: The statement is signed by the Association of European Cancer Leagues, the European Alcohol Policy Alliance, the European Health Alliance on Alcohol, the European Heart Network and the Standing Committee of European Doctors.
Advertisement
POLITICAL ADVERTISEMENT
**A message from EFPIA: Europe needs to compete for investment in the next generation of medicines. The Biotech Act is an opportunity to strengthen the incentives companies need to choose Europe for R&D investment. Extending supplementary protection certificate (SPC) could increase European R&D investment tenfold, helping attract more research and clinical trials, and supporting the development of new medicines in Europe. Read more.**
Sponsor: European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA)
The political advertisement is linked to the EU Biotech Act
WHILE WE'RE TALKING ABOUT HEART HEALTH: The Commission announced Monday it adopted a proposal for a Council recommendation to tackle cardiovascular diseases, which are Europe’s biggest killer, claiming 1.7 million lives a year. The recommendations include more health checks; tackling health inequality by ensuring checks are available and affordable; and encouraging member states to consider personalized prevention and appropriate vaccination advice. Health literacy was also an important tool for empowering Europeans to better understand the value of regular check-ups, the Commission said. The full details are here.
US TARIFFS
D-DAY (AGAIN): Section 232 U.S. tariffs of up to 100% on pharmaceuticals and their ingredients come into effect today for companies that haven’t struck deals with the Trump administration. These deals secure temporary tariff-free access for their products and ingredients while also imposing price controls in the U.S. These so-called most-favored-nation deals also bring U.S. prices for some branded medicines roughly in line with European prices.
Most exposed: Mid-sized European biotech and specialty pharma companies that haven’t signed agreements are the most exposed, according to Diederik Stadig, a health care economist at Dutch bank ING. A handful of biotechs signed agreements last month, bringing the total number of agreements to 26 — so we could expect to see more deals land.
The small print: EU-origin medicines will face a 15% tariff cap under the EU-U.S. Turnberry deal.
Solutions needed: EUCOPE’s Secretary General, Alexander Natz, said there needed to be a sustainable transatlantic solution that safeguarded patient access, investment, and innovation to avoid further trade escalation. Pharma tariffs and the medicine pricing debate “has very real consequences for companies and patients,” he told Morning Health Care. “MFN agreements may provide certainty for individual manufacturers, but they do not resolve the broader challenges facing the European pharmaceutical ecosystem.”
Meanwhile: Generic and biosimilar manufacturers are exempt from all U.S. tariffs that have so far impacted the medicines sector. Adrian van den Hoven, head of generics lobby Medicines for Europe, said tariffs on medicines were counterproductive and called for off-patent medicines to remain exempt.
Advertisement
He pointed out: “Medicines for Europe’s analysis shows that for almost 700 active pharmaceutical ingredients approved in the U.S., Europe is the sole supplier, underlining the importance of maintaining open trade in medicines and pharmaceutical ingredients.”
Remember: A standard zero-tariff rate was agreed upon by World Trade Organization members more than three decades ago for ethical reasons.
And: This comes as the Council of the EU adopted a pharma package aimed at improving patients’ access to medicines and boosting competitiveness. The package includes eight years of data protection for companies that bring new medicines to market, granting them exclusive rights to pre-clinical tests and clinical trials. You can read the full details here.
BIOTECH ACT
WE MEET AGAIN: Shadow rapporteurs will meet to discuss the Biotech Act as they search for compromise amendments on controversial issues like patent extensions. Officials have been meeting for weeks to comb through the legislation line by line and cut through some 3,000 proposed amendments.
Not what we wanted: The meeting brings together industry representatives, experts and European Commission officials for panels on supplementary protection certificates, clinical trial regulations and financing. But some MEPs aren’t happy that the roundtables are being offered in lieu of an independent study.
But, but, but: Although one official previously told us that the EPRS had considered commissioning an external assessment; however, no one had signed off on a tender due to the timeframe and complexity. Catch up on the full story here.
Advertisement
It’s not just some MEPs who raised questions: Civil society groups have criticized the organizers for not including their voices on the panel. “Sidelining civil society, who would be most affected by the new SPC rules, has left us perplexed,” said Ancel·la Santos Quintano, head of one health at BEUC. “Consumer organisations are happy to engage in the discussions about fairer alternatives to measures that risk delaying the arrival of cheaper medicines on the market, instead of playing gooseberry.”
Unfair: A Parliament official told Morning Health Care that it is a “bit unfair to complain,” and that the organizers needed to be more selective due to time concerns. “Given that the panels only last for one hour each, we couldn't include all organisations that have an opinion on the issue,” they said. “We've always tried to create a very broad spectrum to touch every angle possible.”
Our turn next: “European doctors hope the European Parliament will provide an equally meaningful opportunity for civil society to share its views on the development of the Biotech Act,” said Sarada Das, secretary-general of the Standing Committee of European Doctors.
WHAT WE’RE READING
Reuters: Congo’s Ebola outbreak has eclipsed 8,000 cases.
**A message from EFPIA: The Biotech Act introduces a 12-month SPC extension for biotechnology products and Advanced Therapy Medicinal Products (ATMPs). But in its current form, it risks falling short of providing a meaningful and competitive incentive that can influence company investment decisions. A sufficiently broad scope, combined with flexible, workable and non-cumulative eligibility criteria, could make a significant difference. Under the Commission proposal, an estimated 2,200 additional patients could be enrolled in clinical trials, with 2 additional innovative medicines developed over 15 years. With broader scope and eligibility, this could rise to 24,500 additional places for patients in clinical trials and 18 additional medicines developed in the EU. The estimated impact on healthcare spending of a 12-month extension with broad scope and eligibility? Just 0.07%. Read more.**
Sponsor: European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA)
