articles.title: Myanmar army airstrike kills 49 and injures 58 others in market in opposition-controlled Rakhine state
articles.body:
The Arakan Army accused the army of using fighter jets to drop bombs near the civilian market around noon on Monday, killing many people. The incident is the latest in a continued territorial fight between Myanmar’s ruling junta and the Arakan Army, which controls the state of Rakhine.
An airstrike carried out by Myanmar’s military near a market in territory controlled by a powerful rebel group killed at least 49 people and wounded 58 others on Monday, according to representatives of the group and a rescue official.
The attack in western Rakhine state was the latest in a series of deadly airstrikes against pro-democracy resistance forces and ethnic armed groups across the country.
Myanmar has been in turmoil since the military seized power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi on 1 February, 2021, triggering widespread opposition.
After security forces suppressed peaceful protests with lethal force, many opponents of military rule took up arms, plunging large parts of the country into conflict.
Monday’s attack occurred in Kyauktaw township, about 340 kilometres west of Mandalay, the country’s second-largest city, according to the Arakan Army, a powerful ethnic armed group based in Rakhine which controls Kyauktaw.
The Arakan Army said in a statement released early on Tuesday that a fighter jet dropped two bombs near a local market around noon, killing vendors, shoppers and pedestrians. The group said 58 other people were injured, 22 of them critically. Details of the attack could not be independently verified.
The statement said the group "will take effective retaliatory measures soon against the individuals and organisations directly responsible for the attacks involving deliberate airstrikes that have caused mass casualties.”
Wai Hun Aung, a senior rescue official in Rakhine, confirmed the casualties to The Associated Press, citing rescue workers at the scene. He said the market was the region’s main wholesale centre, drawing traders and shoppers from across the state.
“This is one of the most severe airstrikes in Rakhine,” he said. Photos and videos posted on social media showed buildings on fire, damaged vehicles and parts of a nearby bridge destroyed.
The military did not immediately comment on the attack, though it has routinely stated in previous instances that it strikes only legitimate military targets and has accused resistance groups of terrorism.
The Arakan Army is the well-trained and well-armed military wing of a movement seeking autonomy for Rakhine’s ethnic minority from Myanmar’s central government.
It launched an offensive in Rakhine in November 2023 and has since captured a strategically important regional military headquarters and 14 of the state’s 17 townships.
The military has imposed severe restrictions on trade routes since fighting intensified in Rakhine, worsening food shortages.
In December, a military airstrike on a hospital in Rakhine’s Mrauk-U township killed at least 34 people and wounded 80 others.

articles.title: ‘Yes, I regret going’: Russian IT specialist returned to Russia to visit his ailing father and was charged with treason over €30 sent to his ex-girlfriend in Ukraine.
articles.body:
‘Yes, I regret going’: Russian IT specialist returned to Russia to visit his ailing father and was charged with treason over €30 sent to his ex-girlfriend in Ukraine.
A court in Russia’s Komi Republic recently sentenced philosophy instructor Nikolai Zyuzev to seven years in a penal colony. He left Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine began but returned to his home village in 2025. He was detained there and charged with treason. Zyuzev is far from the only Russian who has returned home and ended up behind bars. Memorial has counted at least 40 such cases since 2022. Meduza briefly recounts some of the most telling cases.
The purpose of this article is simple: We have no right to judge the circumstances that compel our readers abroad to travel to Russia. We want to remind them to weigh the risks and take precautions.
Who Memorial says should avoid traveling to Russia
- If you have donated to any Ukrainian initiatives or to charities helping Ukraine and Ukrainian refugees
- If you have donated to the Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK) or any other organizations designated extremist, terrorist, or undesirable in Russia
- If you have had contact with such organizations, including before they received those designations in Russia
- If you took part in opposition or antiwar protests in Russia, or were detained, penalized for a noncriminal offense, or summoned to a police station for questioning over those protests, or if a local police officer came to warn you against joining unauthorized protests
- If you wrote opposition or antiwar posts or comments on any social media platform, even if you later deleted them — or think you did
- If, after leaving Russia, you posted photos or videos of yourself taking part in protests abroad, or photos of Ukrainian symbols, on social media
- If you are a Ukrainian citizen, live or have lived in Ukraine for a long time, or have been there since Russia’s full-scale invasion began
- If you have not checked the wanted persons database or obtained a certificate of no criminal record through the Gosuslugi government services portal to make sure no criminal investigation has been opened against you
Nikolai Zyuzev
Zyuzev is a philosophy Ph.D. who studies the work of Pitirim Sorokin. He moved to Canada in the 2000s, taught there, and became a citizen, but returned to work in Komi in the second half of the 2010s. Friends describe him as a “classical liberal” who was also interested in preserving the Komi language and culture.
In a 2023 article for the Canadian magazine Maclean’s, Zyuzev said he was trying to create an educational platform about Russia’s Indigenous peoples. “We see an opportunity created by Putin’s catastrophic invasion of Ukraine: Indigenous peoples have been disproportionately affected by the war — both on the front lines and through conscription into the Russian army. […] We hope demands for decolonization will grow louder and the Kremlin will lose control over the republics,” Zyuzev said.
He had lived in Lithuania since 2022, but traveled to his home village of Podyelsk in the summer of 2025. His friends do not know exactly why he decided to return. Perhaps he missed home and thought “no one was particularly interested in him.” After his return, Zyuzev disappeared. More than a year later, it emerged that he had been sentenced to seven years for treason over a project he had created to “liberate” Russia’s Indigenous peoples. Developed with foreign grants, the project was aimed at undermining Russia’s sovereignty, according to the country’s Federal Security Service.
Alexander Lunyov
Lunyov became known in 2012 after buying an abandoned water tower from the Tomsk authorities. He spent eight years and more than eight million rubles renovating it. He moved into the tower in the fall of 2020 but did not live there long. He moved to the Czech Republic in 2022, though he had no intention of giving up his home in Tomsk.
“Ideally, I’d make a little more money and put more into the building. We’d restore the building’s exterior and make a few other improvements. My wife and I would still come stay in the tower at least twice a year,” he told Moskvich Mag in 2025.
Lunyov was detained in Tomsk in August 2026. He had traveled from Prague to his hometown with his wife and their daughter, who was only a few months old. Perhaps he wanted to introduce her to relatives in Russia. Lunyov was accused of donating 7,000 rubles to Alexey Navalny’s FBK. He is under criminal investigation for financing extremist activity and faces up to eight years in prison.
Mikhail Loshchinin
An IT specialist, Loshchinin was born in Moscow, spent his childhood and youth in Ukraine, and had lived in Europe since the late 1990s. In the summer of 2025, he rode his motorcycle to Russia to visit his father, who had suffered a heart attack. As Loshchinin crossed the border from Latvia into Russia, border guards found many contacts in Ukraine on his phone. He still had friends and relatives there. He had not deleted anything from his phone before traveling to Russia — apparently, he did not think he had anything to hide.
He was detained and charged with treason over a 30-euro transfer he sent to his former girlfriend in Ukraine in 2022. “Do I regret going? That’s a rhetorical question under the circumstances. I lost the best job I ever had, all my money and investments, and my apartment; my abductions have taken a terrible toll on my mother’s health; and I’m rapidly losing my health, my teeth, and my eyesight. The deputy head of the investigative department says I’ll get 18 years in prison because I won’t admit guilt. Yes, I regret going,” Loshchinin wrote from pretrial detention.
Eduard Sharlot
A singer and blogger, Sharlot left for Armenia in 2022. He openly condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and made videos mocking the Russian authorities and their propaganda. This drew the attention of pro-government informers in Russia, including Yekaterina Mizulina and the Sorok Sorokov movement. Nevertheless, Sharlot said in 2023 that he was returning to Russia. He was detained and sentenced to five and a half years in prison on charges of “rehabilitating Nazism” and offending religious sensibilities. He asked to be sent to the front in Ukraine but was refused.
Pavel Vladimirov
An anarchist from Voronezh, Vladimirov left Russia for Kazakhstan in 2024 at age 18. He was detained there at Russia’s request and held in custody pending extradition for a year, the maximum allowed. According to human rights advocates, his father came to pick him up when he was released and persuaded him to return to Russia, saying, “At least he’ll be nearby, even if they put him in prison.” In Russia, Vladimirov was sentenced to nine years for attempting to join “foreign armed formations.”
Oleg Varyukhin
A native of Norilsk, Varyukhin had lived in Ukraine since 1999 and ran a perfume business there. In 2026, he flew to Russia from Moldova to visit relatives. He was detained at the airport and held through four consecutive detention orders on petty hooliganism charges — a “carousel” of arrests. Afterward, Varyukhin was charged with treason. Mediazona reported that the case stemmed from taxes he had paid to Ukraine as a sole proprietor.
Warning: The paragraph below contains profanity.
Anastasia Ronzhina
Ronzhina lived in Argentina and returned to Russia in the summer of 2026 to visit her mother, who had been diagnosed with cancer. She was detained at the airport and is now in pretrial detention on charges of calling for terrorism. She faces up to seven years in prison. The details of her case are unknown, but Memorial said that, according to some accounts, the charge involves a Telegram comment saying, “Fucking hit the State Duma.”
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: NATO sets out plan to make allied forces quantum ready
articles.body:
NATO has published a public summary of a quantum technology roadmap intended to speed up the adoption of quantum computing, communication and sensing across the alliance and allied armed forces, and to guard against the disruption those technologies could cause in the hands of others, according to NATO.
Allies approved the roadmap on 30 July, with the summary released on Tuesday. It builds on the alliance’s Quantum Strategy of 2023 and concentrates on the three branches of the field, alongside how each interacts with other dual-use technologies including artificial intelligence, space and next generation communication networks.
Delivery runs through the Transatlantic Quantum Community and its industry network, working with industry and academia. That body met in Washington on 24 and 25 September, where according to NATO the discussion covered how advances in quantum computing could affect secure communications, critical infrastructure, intelligence, strategic stability and decision making in a crisis, along with what the convergence of artificial intelligence and quantum means for defence.
The same meeting looked at positioning, navigation and timing, and at sensing, in light of the Questor 26 experimentation campaign run earlier this month at La Spezia by the NATO Centre for Maritime Research and Experimentation together with the industry network.
A sufficiently capable quantum computer would break the public key cryptography that protects most military and civil communications, which is why encrypted traffic intercepted today is worth storing against the day it can be read, and why allied governments have been migrating towards post-quantum algorithms. Quantum sensing runs the other way, offering navigation that does not depend on satellite signals at all, which matters a great deal to forces operating where those signals are jammed or spoofed as a matter of routine, as they now are across the Baltic and the Black Sea.
The Transatlantic Quantum Community welcomed Belgium and Bulgaria at the Washington meeting, bringing it to 24 allies alongside six partner nations. The Netherlands took the chair in May for a year with Canada as vice-chair, and the body, established in 2024, is an informal and non-binding grouping of experts drawn from national governments, industry, academia, funding bodies and research institutions rather than a decision-making forum.
Britain has been working the same ground nationally for some years, and the Ministry of Defence and the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory have run quantum navigation trials at sea and in the air over recent years, and the National Quantum Strategy commits public funding across the decade with defence as one of the intended beneficiaries. The Royal Navy’s experimentation vessel XV Patrick Blackett has been used for trials of this kind.
The full roadmap summary is published on the NATO site alongside the announcement, and the alliance gives no figures for what the work will cost or timescales for when any of the capability is expected to reach the field.

articles.title: Iran awaits US response to proposal as Trump denies concessions
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran waits for US response to peace proposals as Trump denies making concessions
Iran put forward ideas for reaching a new peace agreement with the US through Qatari mediators, Iranian state media reported on Monday, while US President Donald Trump denied reports that he had offered Tehran concessions to end the war.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi is currently in New York, where he has discussed a number of ideas with Qatari mediators to be presented to the US. He denied reports that Tehran had shown flexibility on the nuclear issue.
On Tuesday, Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed Al-Ansari said efforts were still underway to arrange meetings between the US and Iran.
“We are carrying messages between the parties to build common ground,” he said.
Al-Ansari, however, warned against Iranian threats to target infrastructure in Gulf countries, saying: “Iranian attacks on our countries are unjustified aggression, and we did not choose to be a party to this war.”
He added that “any threat to infrastructure is a violation of the principles of international law and good-neighbourly relations.”
Araghchi said a seven-point plan had been conveyed to the US through Qatari mediators, adding that Iran was still waiting for an official response despite Trump’s statements.
Following a report by Axios that Trump was prepared to ease sanctions on Iran and release frozen funds in exchange for concrete steps regarding Iran’s nuclear programme, the US president angrily denied the claim.
“This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING,” he wrote on his Truth Social platform on Monday.
Araghchi added that Iranian officials met one of the Qatari mediators on Monday and discussed ideas for paving the way towards implementing Iran’s conditions. He said the mediators would present the ideas to the US side before conveying Washington’s final response to Tehran.
Araghchi expressed hope that the US response would arrive on Tuesday, adding that he would leave New York for Tehran within hours and that Qatari mediators would know how to deliver the response as soon as they received it.
The Iranian foreign minister added that Iran’s position on its nuclear programme remained unchanged and that Tehran had shown no flexibility on the issue.
He said the current discussions were limited to the Strait of Hormuz and that the strategic waterway would only be reopened if a series of conditions communicated by Iran were met.
According to officials who spoke to the Associated Press, the proposal currently under discussion involves reopening the Strait of Hormuz and lifting the US blockade on Iranian ports, followed by the lifting of sanctions on Iran.
A draft of the agreement indicates that the strait would be reopened under a separate understanding discussed between Iran and Oman, with no fees imposed on ships. The agreement would temporarily regulate the movement of vessels through the strategic waterway.

articles.title: No uncrewed systems used in warship sinking off Scotland
articles.body:
No uncrewed systems took part at any stage of the exercise that ended with the sinking of the decommissioned American frigate USS Klakring off the Hebrides, the officer who commanded it has confirmed, in an event the Ministry of Defence had originally scoped around uncrewed underwater work.
Captain Kelechi Ndukwe, commander of Task Force 65 at Naval Station Rota, was asked at a media roundtable whether unmanned systems were used at all during Atlantic Thunder 2026. “No, they were not,” he said.
The Request for Information the department issued in August 2025, inviting industry to take part, had placed considerable weight on exactly that. It sought high-resolution scanning at depths down to 6,000 feet, autonomous and AI-driven mission tools, long-endurance and low-signature platforms, new approaches to launch and recovery, and communication systems able to work where bandwidth is constrained. Its stated outcomes covered accelerating national and bilateral maritime uncrewed systems development, driving interoperability and interchangeability, and promoting the operational exploitation of those capabilities to fill maritime capability gaps.
That document described Atlantic Thunder 26 as “a US-UK multi-domain exercise designed to validate SUW kill chains, build resilient kill webs and deliver strategic messaging through kinetic demonstration that will take place off the coast of the Hebrides in Scotland from 11th-22nd May 2026.” It was also explicit that the event was not a shop window. “Whilst AT26 presents opportunities to showcase technology, and for Industry contributions to be highlighted during the exercise to an appropriate audience, it must be understood that this is a development exercise,” the department stated. “The focus will be on accelerating capability delivery by addressing the capability blockers listed.”
Battle damage assessment in the event came from sensors fitted to the hull before it was towed out. Naval Surface Warfare Center Carderock and Naval Information Warfare Center Pacific installed the equipment, and Sixth Fleet said the data gathered will be used in post-exercise assessments to identify system failures rapidly, determine repair needs and strengthen the navy’s response in a real engagement. Ndukwe told the UK Defence Journal that the results would be processed over the following months and shared between the two navies.
The hull now lies in what the captain described as a deep valley off the Hebrides, at a depth the earlier planning documents put at around 6,000 feet, as we reported. Whether uncrewed vehicles will be used to survey it has not been set out.
Both navies have been moving work towards uncrewed platforms elsewhere, and the Royal Navy has been running mine countermeasures through remotely operated and autonomous systems as the Hunt and Sandown classes leave service, has trialled autonomous boats on the Clyde, and has £1.3 billion committed for autonomous ships and underwater vessels under the Defence Investment Plan, a figure Wes Streeting restated from the Labour Party conference platform this week. Atlantic Bastion and the associated seabed and anti-submarine programmes rest on the same technologies.
What the exercise did test was long-range strike from crewed platforms across several domains. USS Paul Ignatius fired an anti-surface variant of the Standard Missile 6 at the greatest range available, the submarine USS Massachusetts finished the frigate with a Mark 48 Advanced Capability Torpedo, HMS Portland fired the Naval Strike Missile and a Wildcat launched Sea Venom, with P-8 maritime patrol aircraft from both countries and United States Air Force F-15E Strike Eagles also taking part.
Ndukwe said reach was the difference between this exercise and the last one held off the same range in 2022. “In past iterations of Atlantic Thunder, we weren’t able to test at the longest range, and I think that’s the biggest change from previous exercises,” he said, citing the involvement of the air forces and the technologies developed over the four years the event spent in planning.
Planning has begun on a further iteration, which the two navies aim to run in 2028.

articles.title: Analytic Philosophy and McCarthyism: A New Look (guest post)
articles.body:
To what extent is the “the story about the analytic turn” in philosophy a story about politics?
There’s been an increased discussion in recent years of externalist explanations of philosophy, and one such explanation that has gotten a fair amount of attention lately is the idea that McCarthyist anti-communism in the United States in the middle of the 20th Century played a significant role in analytic philosophy’s emerging dominance in the discipline at the time.
In the following guest post, Sander Verhaegh of Tilburg University, shows how the picture is quite a bit more complicated than that, casting doubt on how much the “McCarthyist thesis” can explain.
The post grew out of research Professor Verhaegh conducted for his just-published book, Logical Positivism: An American History (also here and here).
Analytic Philosophy and McCarthyism: A New Look
by Sander Verhaegh
How to explain the analytic turn in American philosophy? One controversial thesis, regularly discussed in the blogosphere, is that analytic philosophy’s dominance is a product of McCarthyism. On this view, anti-communist repression forced philosophers to abandon socially-engaged, humanistic modes of inquiry, and to a replace them with a technical, ‘politically neutral’ approach. John McCumber develops the theory in two of his books and the hypothesis recently resurfaced in publications by Christoph Schuringa and by Robert Hanna, who likens postwar analytic philosophy to “McCarthy-style anti-communist, big-capitalist politics”.
Critics have pushed back hard. Richard Hudelson and Robert Evans argue that McCumber “fails to give a historically or philosophically coherent account” of the analytic turn, while E. J. Spode compares Schuringa’s book to “A Turd in the Punchbowl”. Some contend that the McCarthyist thesis ignores simultaneous analytic turns in Canada, Australia, and the United Kingdom, such that it offers an “American explanation for … a pan-Anglophone phenomenon”. Others point out that some of the best-known analytic philosophers of the period, Bertrand Russell and Rudolf Carnap, were hardly the apolitical figures the thesis requires; while the most notorious anti-Communist witch-hunters, Arthur Lovejoy and Sidney Hook, were humanist philosophers who had studied with William James and John Dewey.
In this post, I discuss archival evidence that sheds new light on the question. In the last eight years, I spent much of my research time in archives for a book on the history of twentieth-century American philosophy, working through a wealth of material from the period: departmental records, diaries, correspondence, personnel files, and hundreds of newspapers and magazines. The book, Logical Positivism: An American History, reconstructs how émigré positivists and their American students and allies rose to dominance at private and public universities; and it shows that the story about the analytic turn is more complicated than the McCarthyist thesis suggests. In what follows, I argue that the Cold War did play a role in the development of American philosophy, albeit in various unexpected ways ignored by proponents of the McCarthyist view. At the same time, I argue that it was not the only factor, let alone a sufficient explanation, for the analytic turn.
The McCarthyist Thesis
Before discussing the evidence, let us get clear about the explanandum. Though there seem to be as many variants of the McCarthyist thesis as there are historians who have written about the period, no one argues that analytic philosophy itself is a product of the Cold War. Proponents and opponents agree that the analytic tradition predates the McCarthy era, in Europe and in the United States, even if anti-communist pressures may have changed its character in the 1950s. The central question is not to explain analytic philosophy’s presence. It is to understand its hegemonic position by the early 1960s, since American departments and journals of philosophy had been dominated by non-analytic schools and movements before the Second World War.
Naturally, it is difficult, if not impossible, to sharply define what does and does not count as ‘analytic philosophy’. Still, even a cursory look at the composition of American philosophy departments, curricula, and journals, as well as lists of APA presidents and Carus lecturers reveals that something changed in this period. Nor is this an ahistorical projection. At the time, philosophers regularly observed and discussed the rapid transformation of their discipline (more on this below), even if it took a while before ‘analytic philosophy’ became the generally accepted label for the newly dominant approach.
Second, if we are to evaluate the McCarthyist thesis, we need to get clear about the supposed victims of anti-communist repression. Few people will deny that (former) communists and Marxist scholars were pushed out of the profession. The central question is whether the Red Scare also affected pragmatists, phenomenologists, and ‘continental’ philosophers more generally. McCumber and Schuringa answer in the affirmative, arguing that anti-communist pressures blocked out any alternative to the Cold War paradigm; Joshua Rayman and James A. Good deny that pragmatism was a target. George Reisch, finally, argues for the more subtle thesis that McCarthyism played a role but affected analytic and non-analytic philosophers alike. Whereas many logical positivists and their American allies had been politically engaged in the 1930s, they turned to the “icy slopes of logic” in the years thereafter.
Finally, we need to get clear about the mechanisms through which the Cold War reshaped American philosophy. Since only a few, relatively minor philosophers were direct victims of McCarthyite investigations, proponents need a story about how the Red Scare affected the composition of journals and departments of philosophy. Most agree that anti-communist pressures created “a “climate of fear”, stimulating philosophers, journal editors, and university administrators to self-curate to prevent public controversy. But some add that there were carrots as well as sticks: Analytic philosophers were showered with funding and cushy advisory positions at institutes like RAND Corporation. Lastly, McCumber believes that there are conceptual connections between analytic philosophy and Cold War ideology. He argues that while pragmatists dealt with context-dependent problems of men, analytic philosophers saw truth as a property of sentences independent of context, thereby echoing the absolutist modes of thinking that were dominant in the period.
Analytic Philosophy Before the Red Scare
Let us turn to the evidence, starting with the state of American philosophy before the Cold War. Now, even if we accept that the McCarthyist thesis seeks to explain analytic philosophy’s dominance, not its existence or emergence, the timing is awkward: Analytic philosophy already had a solid foothold in the 1920s and 1930s. When Herbert Feigl, the first of the logical positivists to emigrate to the United States, arrived at Harvard in September 1930, it was already considered a flourishing “center” for logic-infused philosophy. Feigl found American colleagues developing ideas that were, in his words, “barely distinguishable” from the Vienna Circle’s scientific world conception, and he regularly attended meetings of a group of talented young philosophers, including W. V. Quine, Susanne Langer, and Nelson Goodman, writing that they were “almost always discuss[ing] logic” and it was “almost like in Vienna!” (letters from Dec. 6, 1930 and Apr. 5, 1931).
Harvard was not an isolated case. Even if American departments were dominated by non-analytic philosophers at the professor level, there is much archival evidence that the new generation had started to adopt the style of philosophy that was in vogue in Cambridge, Prague, Vienna, Warsaw, and Berlin. C. I. Lewis wrote that “logical posi[vi]sm easily takes the first place in the interest and the discussions of our students” (letter, Dec. 1934). Cecil Currie was surprised how much the analytic movement had “caught on among the younger generation” (letter, May 1944), and an advisor for Princeton’s department wrote about “the trend which takes the students at this time to Wittgenstein and other positivists” (letter, Apr. 1947). Even Kant-scholar Charles Hendel, who deeply opposed the trend, wrote that “we ‘older boys’ have to take cognisance … of the enthusiasm and conviction of the younger logicians” (letter, May 1951).
These historical eye-witness reports are supported by bibliometric studies. A network analysis of the most-mentioned philosophers in American journals in the 1940s, for example, reveals that the literature of the period can be divided into at least two, roughly equally-sized clusters of discussion: (1) a set of literature mentioning mostly émigré positivists, Cambridge analysts, and young American philosophers such as Ernest Nagel and Charles Stevenson; and (2) a cluster mentioning American professors who felt that the focus on “logical clarity is producing a kind of sterility that has largely destroyed [philosophy’s] cultural value” (letter by Charles Cory, 1945). The most striking difference between the two clusters is a demographic one: The median birth year of U.S.-based philosophers in what we would now call the ‘analytic’ cluster is 1899, whereas the median birth year of the U.S.-based philosophers in the second cluster is 1882— a difference of seventeen years!
Considering this generational divide, it is much less puzzling that analytic philosophy boomed after the Second World War. In the 1930s, analytic philosophy was already popular among students and junior scholars. But this was not reflected in the hiring of the period. American universities faced severe budget cuts due to the Great Depression (in the 1930s) and the War (the 1940s), so there was little space to hire analytic philosophers. Only when departments could expand in the 1950s, they had the opportunity to catch up. Coincidentally, this is exactly the period when the older generation, educated in what they called “the Golden Age of American Philosophy” (the 1900s and 1910s), retired. In consequence, it was the new, more analytically-minded generation that could steer American philosophy in a different direction, a period when the U.S. student population grew from 2.7 million to 8.0 million in two decades. A study of the growth of eleven prominent philosophy departments estimates that they increased from 6.3 to 17.3 faculty on average, meaning that there was much space for new hires.
Appointments in the McCarthy Era
Even if the timing and the swiftness of the analytic turn are partly explained by a generational shift and a fifteen-year dip in the job market, this does not entail that McCarthyism played no role in the process. So let us turn to academic hiring in more detail. Now, if the anti-communist climate of fear was an important factor in the analytic turn, one would expect deans, department chairs, and university presidents to reflect on the risks involved in hiring pragmatists, humanists, and existentialists irrespective of the candidates’ political ideas and activities. Yet, in my archival research on the hiring procedures of ten departments of philosophy, including both private (Columbia, Cornell, Harvard, Princeton, and Yale) and public universities (UC Berkeley, UMich, UMN, UIowa, and UPenn), I have not found a single example of a philosopher or administrator raising doubts about a candidate because of their philosophical affiliation.
Of course not every meeting is recorded. Moreover, it is well-known that repressive environments can be governed by tacit agreements on how to avoid public controversy. Yet it seems unlikely that the supposed political risks involved in appointing a pragmatist or a phenomenologist did not leave a single trace in thousands of pages of dossiers about possible hires, particularly since administrators often did voice concerns about other ‘liabilities’ involving race and religion. When Yale considered hiring Paul Weiss, the head of department openly shared his worry that he would be a risk because he was likely to have some of the “deficiencies that Jewish people labor”, most notably a “lack of social discretion” (letter, Oct. 2, 1945). And when Princeton was searching a new full professor, the president was openly warned not to appoint a Catholic because members of “the Roman hierarchy” could not “avoid being illiberal” (letter, May 1948). While the records show that some candidates were considered a liability because of their race or religious affiliation, I have encountered no discussions of potential hires who were considered a risk because they were pragmatists or phenomenologists.
Second, it is important to note that all these departments kept hiring non-analytic philosophers. In some cases, it was even an explicit criterion that a position should be filled by a pragmatist or continental philosopher. Jacques Barzun, provost at Columbia, urged the philosophy department to establish “a balance between ‘analysts’ and ‘humanists’” (letter, May 1960) and when Princeton could appoint two full professors, the president and the department agreed that one of the appointees had to be “broadly humanistic in his philosophical orientation” and that the other should be “logical and scientific in his outlook” (memo, Dec. 1954).
Naturally, these conclusions do not apply to philosophers who were suspect because of their political activities. Irving Copi’s personnel file at the University of Michigan contains a letter from William Frankena, defending the former Troskyite because he had “entirely renounced his questionable connections, opinions, and activities” (letter, Sep. 1948). And when the University of Minnesota refused to renew the contract of Forrest Wiggins in 1951, the department’s first Black instructor publicly announced that it was because his “Communist line” had cost the university money in the state legislature (Star Tribune, Dec. 13, 1951).
Cultural Momentum
Finally, let us turn the broader cultural conversation about philosophy. The standard focus on McCarthyism is rather one-sided because it has led historians to overlook other important elements of America’s cultural moment. The 1950s were not just marked by Cold War anxieties. It was also a decade of cultural optimism about science and technology. Science had not just helped the United States win the Second World War. It had also improved the life of average Americans through the introduction of new medical treatments such as polio vaccines, synthetic antibiotics, and ultrasound monitoring; as well as exciting consumer products such as portable television, credit cards, and long-playing vinyl records.
In order to understand the analytic turn, in particular the success of logical positivism, one has to incorporate this cultural optimism about modern science. Today, logical positivism is often associated with the dark sides of science and technology. Positivism is equated with the value-free conception of science that helped universities justify research that was used to sow death and destruction in Vietnam. But it is important to realize that these associations only emerged in the late 1960s, when the protest generation identified positivism as the ideology of the military-industrial complex. In the 1950s, logical positivism was still widely regarded as a model of modern scientific thinking, even in popular newspapers and magazines. Wallace David, a minister and gay rights activist, could note that we live “in a scientific age” and describe himself as a member of the “school of ‘logical positivism’” (ONE Magazine, June 1954). An Alabama newspaper could positively comment on a proposal to add logic to the state school curriculum, noting how comforting it would be to “listen to sermons or to political speeches and be able to say with the logical positivists that they fall short” (The Anniston Star, Mar. 15, 1957). And a political columnist could praise John F. Kennedy’s actions during the Cuban Missile Crisis because he displayed “a harshness of which the intellect only of the logical empiricist intellectual is capable” (Times Argus, Dec. 3, 1962). None of these references reflect any real engagement with positivist views or arguments. But it does provide a window on analytic philosophy’s cultural momentum: logical positivism came to exemplify a modern scientific attitude in a period when ninety-four percent of U.S. citizens felt that science was making their lives “healthier, easier, and more comfortable”.
Pragmatism, meanwhile, often got negative press, in particular during the Sputnik crisis of 1957. After the USSR successfully launched the first satellite, American media were quick to blame the school system, noting that Russian children spent much more time studying science and mathematics. And some of them held the pragmatists responsible considering their outsized influence on American education. E. F. Hutton commented that the Russians “make their kids study!”, noting that Americans did the same “before John Dewey and his followers said children should never be made to do anything” (Houston Chronicle, Feb. 23, 1958). Admiral H. G. Rickover agreed, proposing to replace Dewey’s idea that “the school is primarily a social institution” with a new, more rigorous “education process” centering on the collection of “factual knowledge” (Omaha World-Herald, Mar. 24, 1958). Analytic philosophy was considered new and exciting and pragmatism old-fashioned and outdated, even if pragmatist ideas and perspectives still played an important role in shaping the views of analytic philosophers like Hilary Putnam, W. V. Quine, Ernest Nagel, and Richard Rorty.
* * *
McCarthyism severely affected the lives of Marxists and (former) socialist philosophers. Yet it played a very limited role in the development of American philosophy. Anti-communist witch-hunts may have led philosophers to be more careful in their political pronouncements. But there is no evidence that the Red Scare significantly impacted the composition of departments of philosophy. At the same time, it would be a mistake to conclude that Cold War culture was not a factor in the analytic turn. Although analytic philosophy had been on the rise since the 1920s, demographic and economic developments had halted its representation in philosophy departments. When analytically-minded philosophers finally had the opportunity to reshape the profession, the conditions were ideal: higher education was growing, the job market was booming, and the American public celebrated science, professionalism, and ‘neutral’ expertise.
A bibliography for this post can be found here. Check out Logical Positivism: An American History here.

articles.title: The enduring friendship between Iran and China
articles.body:
Following threats by the United States to punish and sanction various nations should they engage in aviation cooperation with the Islamic Republic of Iran, the Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson clearly articulated China's position to the American side: China’s stance is consistent and unequivocal—it firmly opposes unilateral and illegal sanctions that lack UN Security Council authorization. The spokesperson added that Beijing opposes such unilateral and illegal sanctions against Tehran and that relations with Iran—including in the aviation sector—will continue. Undoubtedly, China’s message demonstrates that the U.S. cannot use coercion to force all nations to serve its own interests or facilitate the plunder of other countries; thus, China’s stance is of great significance. Evidence indicates that China rejects U.S. unilateralist demands, as it is an independent nation that makes decisions based on its own principles and interests.
In recent months, some foreign media outlets have suggested that relations between China, Russia, and Iran have suffered setbacks—a claim that is inaccurate. In fact, China’s refusal to comply with U.S. policies underscores its principled approach toward Tehran. Iran, China, and Russia are three influential nations in the Eurasian region and play pivotal roles in shaping a future global order based on multilateralism; relations among the three are generally positive and progressing. Indeed, the U.S. is concerned about the expanding cooperation within local and regional pacts involving developing nations—pacts of which Iran is a member. Iran’s participation and cooperation in these agreements can help it overcome economic challenges; consequently, all three nations prioritize their national interests when shaping their mutual relations. At the same time, given the nature of their relations with the United States, neither China nor Russia seeks to halt the advancement of ties with Iran, nor do they fail to honor the mutual commitments existing between us.
Fundamentally, Russia and China insist that international norms serve as the primary basis for decision-making in international forums—particularly the UN Security Council—reasoning that if lawlessness comes to dominate the international community, we will witness increased warmongering in the future. Indeed, the root of the disagreement between China and Russia on one side, and the US, France, and Britain on the other, lies in the issue of adherence to the law and international norms; consequently, they do not support unlawful US actions, such as the sanctions imposed on Iran.
Regarding the decision by certain regional countries to suspend flights to Tehran, I believe they are under intense pressure from the US and, regrettably, are unable to safeguard their own interests. While maintaining air links to Iran generates revenue—serving their own interests—they are sacrificing those interests due to US pressure; however, as Iranian officials have noted, deferring to the US comes at a cost to them, and they may well find their own airports deserted as a result.

articles.title: Air Force, Industry Fear Continuing Resolution Could Hinder CCA Production
articles.body:
The Air Force’s emerging Collaborative Combat Aircraft program would suffer delays if Congress fails to pass a budget before the end of this calendar year, a top service official said Sept. 28.
Brig. Gen. Timothy Helfrich, the portfolio acquisition executive for fighters and advanced aircraft, said the program is ready for production, but advancing to that next stage requires a new budget. “You can’t go do production without production funding,” he said during a Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies appearance. “So that does provide limitations on what we can execute.”
CCAs are the semi-autonomous drone fighters the Air Force believes can bolster its manned fighter force. The first two models—General Atomics Aeronautical Systems’ FQ-42A Vengeance and Anduril Systems’ FQ-44A Fury—are designed for air-to-air strike missions. The objective is for the compact uncrewed CCAs to cost less than $20 million apiece for the airframe, and to rapidly grow the force to include at least 500 in 2032, on its way to at least 1,000 later on.
Fiscal 2027 starts Oct. 1, but Congress failed to pass a budget before taking its recess, instead passing a funding measure that extends appropriations at 2026 levels until Dec. 11. Under such a continuing resolution, new programs, such as CCA production, are not authorized. If Congress fails to pass a budget the government could be forced to shut down. Congress could also vote to extend the CR for a month or more at that time.
Helfrich’s comments echoed concerns raised by Anduril officials at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference in National Harbor, Md., Sept. 14.
Erin Simpson, Anduril’s vice president of strategy execution for air dominance and strike, told reporters in a briefing that the company has worked to get a head start on procurement, including by building a new Arsenal-1 factory in Columbus, Ohio, buying parts in advance, and producing prototype Fury CCAs.
“We will not have a cold start to [launch] production in ’27,” Simpson said. “We will have assets rolling through. That said, even a company like ours can only do so much without procurement dollars.”
When asked about the CR’s potential effect on General Atomics’ production, a company spokesman pointed to a Sept. 21 release that said it is taking on risk by self-funding some of the first FQ-42s, to keep the program moving forward while the Pentagon’s funding is worked out.
“Production of FQ-42 Vengeance is underway on company investment as government funding plans mature, with GA-ASI continuing its longstanding tradition of working at-risk with its own funds to support U.S. procurement planning and prevent delays in delivery,” General Atomics’ statement said. GA-ASI plans to build multiple fighters for its own company aircraft fleet, to invest in inventing new technologies that reduce risk and increase capabilities for its global customers.”
Helfrich said the Air Force’s upcoming Emerald Flag exercise in December at Eglin Air Force Base, Fla., will be a significant demonstration of how far CCAs have come. And it will further the work done by the Air Force’s Experimental Operations Unit to figure out how best to use CCAs in operational environments, and how to operate it under the Agile Combat Employment construct of flying aircraft out of dispersed, small and rough airfields in a future conflict.
“Setting up for Emerald Flag, it’s all hands on deck, but the EOU is central to making that happen,” Helfrich said. “They’re at the heart of taking a capability and making it into something that we can actually integrate into the Air Force.”
Both initial CCA models will fly at Emerald Flag alongside different manned fighters, he said, possibly with multiple CCAs flying at once.
The Air Force announced in July that Anduril’s Fury CCA had fired its first live missile in a test. General Atomics’ Vengeance will soon follow, Helfrich said. Helfrich indicated that test fire would likely happen before Emerald Flag.
General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley declined to say exactly when the first FQ-42A live-fire test may take place, saying only that it would happen by the end of the year.
Helfrich said the FQ-42A’s live-fire test will focus on more than just launching the missile, and will be a test run of the entire process for firing weapons with an autonomous system, while still keeping a human “on the loop.”
“The human has to make the decision to use lethal force, and then go and engage on that target,” Helfrich said. “So we’re talking more like kill chain than we are about [a standard weapon firing] exercise.”

articles.title: China’s AI strategy ‘paradox’ really isn’t one
articles.body:
China’s AI strategy ‘paradox’ really isn’t one
Artificial intelligence is becoming a defining force in economic development, international competition, and national security. While striving to develop more powerful AI systems, China also seeks to determine how they should be governed, shared, and secured in a rapidly changing world.
A technology shaping China – and the world
By June 2026, the number of users of AI products in China had exceeded 500 million, underscoring the technology’s growing reach in one of the world’s largest digital economies. Together with the US, China is a key engine of AI development and innovation. Its domestic choices and international initiatives have consequences well beyond its borders.
At the BRICS summit in New Delhi, Chinese President Xi Jinping advanced proposals for more inclusive AI cooperation, industrial development, and technological exchange. At the same time, State Security Minister Chen Yixin set out a national security perspective that places AI at the center of strategic competition and calls for stronger safeguards.
China’s AI policy combines the pursuit of international openness with domestic security governance. Understanding how Beijing seeks to reconcile these objectives is essential to understanding its ambitions for AI – and the emerging global order around it.
Xi’s BRICS vision: AI as a shared opportunity
Xi’s proposals at the New Delhi summit place AI cooperation within a broader effort to connect technological development with economic growth and international inclusion. The emphasis is on widening access to the capabilities, skills, and industrial networks that make AI economically useful.
China has proposed taking a pioneering role in establishing a BRICS AI open-source community, supporting cooperation on the development and application of large language models, and organizing specialized seminars and training courses. The stated objective is to build an open ecosystem in which countries can exchange knowledge and expand their capacity to develop and use AI.
This approach is particularly relevant for emerging economies. Access to AI requires not only the availability of software, but also computing infrastructure, technical expertise, investment, and the ability to adapt technologies to local needs. Open-source collaboration and skills development can help accessibility, although they cannot by themselves eliminate disparities in resources or technological capabilities.
Xi’s digital industry cooperation initiative extends the same idea into the infrastructure and skills underpinning the digital economy. China has proposed a BRICS digital ecosystem cloud platform, alongside digital skills training, technological exchange, and industrial alignment.
A third proposal focuses on AI-enabled new industrialization. Here, the objective is to deepen cooperation in research and development, practical applications, and industrial and supply chains.
Taken together, these initiatives present AI as a means of expanding productive capacity. For BRICS members, the proposals raise practical questions about how to share expertise, develop compatible infrastructure, and translate technological cooperation into tangible industrial outcomes.
Chen Yixin’s warning
Xi’s international cooperation agenda coincides with a more security-focused assessment from Chen Yixin, China’s minister of state security. In an article published during the summit, Chen described AI as a central arena of global scientific and technological competition and a new front in strategic rivalry among major powers.
Chen’s argument begins with a dual imperative: innovation must be the primary driving force, while security must remain a bottom-line requirement. In this framing, AI is simultaneously an engine of economic and social transformation and a technology capable of changing the conditions of national security.
His assessment identifies several interconnected risks. AI-generated content, including deepfakes and automated online activity, could affect political security by enabling the rapid production and dissemination of misleading information. Chen also warns that AI may transform cyber operations, making it easier to identify vulnerabilities, develop malicious software, and automate elements of complex attacks.
Another concern is the potential for AI-assisted data collection and analysis to amplify espionage and information-security risks. Chen points to the possibility of sensitive government data, commercial secrets, and personal information being gathered or exposed through intelligent crawling, data mining, and profiling.
He also identifies structural challenges: concentration of technological capabilities could deepen inequalities between countries, while AI-driven decision-making could strain existing systems of social governance. In the military sphere, he argues that AI is helping move warfare toward an increasingly intelligent era, with implications for sensing, decision-making, and targeting.
These concerns are not confined to China. Cybersecurity, data protection, misinformation, military applications, and the concentration of technological power are subjects of international debate. What distinguishes Chen’s article is the way it brings them together under a comprehensive national security framework.
From principles to institutions
Chen calls for AI security to be integrated into other key areas of national security, supported by stronger cross-sector cooperation and improved capacity to identify and anticipate emerging risks. He also calls for an AI safety supervision platform, expanded risk assessment and monitoring, and greater investment in fundamental research and core technologies, including computing chips, development frameworks, and application software. His article advocates strengthening AI infrastructure while reducing vulnerabilities associated with dependence on critical technologies.
Chen advocates the implementation of China’s Cybersecurity Law and Counter-Espionage Law, alongside further development of rules addressing AI research, applications, data protection, algorithmic security, and accountability. He also emphasizes public communication and national security awareness.
These measures reflect Beijing’s view that AI governance cannot be separated from overarching questions of technological self-reliance, data control, and national security, and that when it comes to AI, innovation has to be inseparable from oversight.
A global governance agenda
China’s domestic security priorities sit alongside an international agenda that predates the New Delhi summit. Its 2023 Global AI Governance Initiative calls for people-centered development, international cooperation, respect for national sovereignty, and broader access to AI technologies. It also advocates risk-based governance, privacy and data protection, human oversight, and greater representation for developing countries.
The initiative supports discussions within the United Nations framework on establishing an international institution for AI governance. Chen’s article echoes several of these themes, describing AI as an international public good and calling for cooperation that helps Global South countries strengthen their technological capabilities and bridge the global intelligence gap.
China recently released its AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0, following earlier versions issued in 2024 and 2025. The updated framework revises risk classifications and adjusts technical and governance measures in response to emerging challenges.
Making openness and security compatible
China’s international and domestic AI agendas may seem to be contradictory, but a country can support international technology exchange while seeking to protect sensitive data, strengthen infrastructure, and manage risks. The challenge is determining where legitimate safeguards end and restrictions on cooperation begin.
For China, the task is to demonstrate that its security framework can support innovation and international engagement without unnecessarily constraining them. For its partners, the task is to assess how cooperation will work in practice: what technologies will be accessible, how data will be protected, and how shared initiatives will be governed.
BRICS member countries have different development priorities, regulatory systems, and strategic interests. A common AI ecosystem will require practical arrangements that accommodate those differences while delivering measurable benefits.
A defining question for the AI era
Xi Jinping’s BRICS proposals and Chen Yixin’s national security assessment capture two dimensions of China’s AI strategy: expanding the technology’s reach internationally while strengthening its governance at home.
AI cooperation could widen access to technological capabilities and support industrial development. Security governance could help address genuine risks involving cyber operations, sensitive data, and increasingly autonomous systems. Yet both agendas also raise questions about implementation, institutional accountability, and the balance between openness and control.
China’s approach will be judged by the practical outcomes it delivers: whether cooperation is genuinely inclusive, whether safeguards are effective and proportionate, and whether international partners can participate on mutually understood terms.
The underlying proposition is that artificial intelligence need not be treated as a domain of zero-sum competition. When innovation is prioritized and security requirements are treated as non-negotiable, the technology can be steered toward benefit for all.

articles.title: Nuclear weapons in space would break law, says Britain
articles.body:
Orbital weapons of both kinds pose a growing threat to the space-based services Britain and its allies depend on, and any attempt to put nuclear weapons in orbit would be highly destabilising and contrary to international law, the Ministry of Defence stated in a written answer.
Lord Coaker, Minister of State at the department, was answering Baroness Bennett of Manor Castle, the Green Party peer, who asked what assessment the government had made of the danger of orbital weapons, kinetic and otherwise, following what she described as the disclosure by the United States of its aggressive space capacity, and what steps ministers plan to take to prevent a new arms race in space.
The minister replied: “The Government recognises that orbital weapons, both kinetic and non-kinetic, pose a growing threat to critical space-based services vital to the UK and its allies. We are concerned by reports of efforts to deploy nuclear weapons in space, which would be highly destabilising and contrary to international law. The Government supports a behaviour-based, risk-reduction approach to maintain a safe, secure and sustainable space environment. We work closely with international partners to promote responsible conduct, uphold existing legal frameworks and prevent escalation.”
He continued: “Through the UK Space Strategy and Defence Investment Plan, the Government is investing in the resilience and protection of UK and allied space assets to ensure freedom of action in space and safeguard long-term sustainability. We remain committed to international cooperation and the development of norms that reduce risk and preserve stability in this increasingly contested domain.”
The same minister had declined a week earlier to say whether Britain itself has anything in orbit. Lord Lee of Trafford, the Liberal Democrat peer, asked on 22 September whether the United Kingdom has any weapons in space, and if not whether there are plans to deploy any.
Coaker replied: “We do not comment on specific Defence capabilities, including whether such capabilities are deployed in space, nor on future operational plans where doing so would risk undermining national security. We do however recognise that space is important to military operations and is becoming more congested, contested, and competitive. The Government is committed to collaborating with allies and partners to promote internationally agreed norms, avoid unintentional escalation and conflict, and ensure that space remains open, safe, and sustainable.”
He added: “In addition, the UK’s national security depends on freedom of action in space, including the ability to protect UK and allied space assets. As set out in the UK Space Strategy and Defence Investment Plan, the Government is investing in capabilities to strengthen resilience and support the protection of UK interests in space, while continuing to operate responsibly and in accordance with international law.”

articles.title: "The message to Moscow is clear" - Rutte makes a new statement on NATO's support for Ukraine
articles.body:
"The message to Moscow is clear" - Rutte makes a new statement on NATO's support for Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Rutte said that Russia had not broken NATO's unity, despite sabotage and drones. The Alliance is strengthening its defence and support for Ukraine.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte called on allies to remain calm and continue supporting Ukraine. He noted that Russia has failed to undermine the alliance’s resolve and halt its support for Ukraine, despite the growing number of acts of sabotage and drone incidents targeting NATO. Rutte said this at a press conference on September 29, UNN reports.
Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against NATO allies. It is trying to weaken our resolve and halt our support for Ukraine. But Russia is failing. It is failing on the battlefield in Ukraine, and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine. Our message to Moscow is clear. We will do more for Ukraine, not less
He noted that "repeated drone incidents on our eastern flank have demonstrated the evolving threat, and we are strengthening our integrated air and missile defense".
"We are adapting and strengthening our posture against drones," the NATO Secretary General said.
Speaking about hybrid attacks, Rutte acknowledged that they "have an impact," but, in his words, NATO has "all options for responding: sometimes visible, sometimes not."
"I am not saying that these malicious actions in the gray zone do not have an impact. They can have an impact, and sometimes they have an obvious impact. What I mean is that we have all options for responding. Sometimes visible, sometimes not, not always public, not always 'tit for tat'," Rutte said.
At the same time, he called on the allies: "Continue strengthening NATO."
"And finally, (...) continue supporting Ukraine, because the best response to any actions in the gray zone of what Russia is doing is more support for Ukraine, not less. Because ultimately, they want to divide us so that we lose focus on Ukraine and start discussing among ourselves what is happening, why, and how it all fits together," the NATO Secretary General stressed.
Remain calm, continue and support Ukraine, support it more, not less, just as we are doing, also thanks to the European Union and the loan to support Ukraine
He also announced "excellent news": "We have reached the threshold of 10 billion when it comes to PURL funds. This is vital for the items supplied from the United States to Ukraine and financed by Canada and European allies, including the European Union, which plays a major role here."
"So all of this is extremely important. We (...) must not be naive about Russia. But they know that we are stronger, and we must ensure, by continuing our investments, that we will also be stronger in two, three, and five years. And that is exactly what we are doing," the Secretary General said.

articles.title: For First Time, US F-35s Will Join Exercise in India
articles.body:
Six U.S. Air Force F-35A fighters and 200-plus Airmen deployed to India on Sept. 26 for their first appearance in a large-scale exercise on Indian soil.
Exercise Tarang Shakti will run from Sept. 26 to Oct. 12, according to the Indian Air Force, with eight countries contributing aircraft. First held in 2024, the exercise is India’s largest multinational aerial training event.
U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor and Pacific Air Forces confirmed the arrival of the F-35s and released images of them at Jodhpur Air Force Station. The aircraft are from the 13th Fighter Squadron at Misawa Air Base, Japan.
This is the first time the USAF has deployed F-35s for an exercise in India, although USAF did previously display the Lightning II at Aero India, a large-scale air show. In 2024, the Air Force sent A-10s to Tarang Shakti in 2024, and USAF has sent F-15s and F-16s to participate in previous editions of Cope India, a major joint air combat exercise.
The U.S. and Indian air forces have built up their interaction in recent years. A B-1 bomber landed in India for the first time for Aero India in 2021, then returned for its first exercise at Cope India 2023. Last year, President Donald Trump suggested the U.S. might eventually sell F-35s to India, but little has been said on that topic since.
On the flip side of U.S.-India relations, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has also worked to build ties with Russia and China. Modi met with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and Chinese Premier Xi Jinping earlier this month at the BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa) summit, at which he stressed better relations with both Russia and China.
The Indian Air Force has an eclectic mix of aircraft, including indigenous HAL Tejas light combat aircraft, Russian Su-30s, French Rafales and Mirage 2000s, American C-17s, and more. Russia has also pitched its new Su-57 fighter to India—the Su-57 and F-35 were both at Aero India in 2025.

articles.title: British Commandos called in air strikes alongside Navy SEALs
articles.body:
Royal Marines from the UK Commando Force guided in attacks by American fast jets and seized a ship at sea during three weeks of maritime special operations training with United States Navy SEALs in Virginia, the Royal Navy stated.
The exercise, codenamed Resolute Strike, was intended to get the two forces operating together as one and to keep the British teams ready for NATO tasking. It ran through close-quarter combat scenarios by day and night, taking in vessel boarding and compound clearance, and finished with a validation exercise mounted from the San Antonio-class amphibious transport dock USS Arlington.
Major George Eatwell, Officer in Command of M Company, 42 Commando, said: “Resolute Strike was not only an exceptional Maritime Special Operations training opportunity, but it also proved vital integration with our US partners, testing interchangeability of tactics, equipment, and processes. Whenever, or wherever we may fight alongside the US in the future, we are now better aligned at the operator level having built those lasting foundational relationships.”
Twenty-seven commandos from M Company travelled to Virginia Beach alongside specialists from 148 Battery, who handle multi-domain fires and targeting, after a month of riverine and jungle raiding in southern Mississippi.
The 148 Battery party worked with SEAL teams at the Navy Dare Bombing Range in North Carolina, a remote facility of 72 square miles, which the Royal Navy compares to the size of Wigan, where American aircrew practise air to surface attack. There the British teams talked in strikes by F-18 Super Hornets against area denial systems including surface-to-air missiles, work that falls under the suppression of enemy air defences. Completing it leaves the battery fully certified to support operations at very high readiness.
M Company forms Special Operations Maritime Task Unit 9 and concentrated on maritime interdiction. According to the Royal Navy, task units of this kind are built to deploy worldwide from hubs ashore or from ships, working alone or folded into a partner force, and each can field one force protection team and two boarding teams, with scout snipers, uncrewed systems, dive teams, explosive ordnance disposal and electronic warfare added as required.
The training began with the two sides exchanging tactics before moving on to close-quarters battle objectives, with teams inserted by helicopter in darkness to take compounds, and more than twenty missions were run across various scenarios.
Attention then turned to the water, where an assault team conducted a vessel takedown at night covering explosive and mechanical methods of entry alongside close quarters marksmanship. In the final week the commandos embarked on USS Arlington for a last mission against an American target vessel, with two Black Hawk helicopters putting a combined British and American team onto the ship to seize it.
Both forces hold Arctic responsibilities for their respective countries, and the Royal Navy says the integration work moves to colder conditions this winter.
42 Commando is based at Bickleigh outside Plymouth and is the Royal Marines unit specialising in maritime operations, including boarding and interdiction work. 148 Battery, part of 29 Commando Regiment Royal Artillery, provides forward observation and joint fires support to the commando force and its members qualify as joint terminal attack controllers, which is what allows them to direct strikes by other nations’ aircraft.
The Commando Force has been the subject of considerable investment, with Wes Streeting restating from the Labour Party conference platform this week that half a billion pounds is going into the force and its drone equipment as it helps defend NATO’s High North.
